speaker: Unknown
title: Devi Opens the Inquiry
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
श्री देव्युवाच ।
श्रुतं देि मया सिं रुद्रयामलसम्भवम् ।
विकभेदमशेषेण सारात्सारविभागश् ॥ १ ॥
transliteration: vijñāna-bhairava-tantram | vijñāna-bhairava-tantram | śrī-devy uvāca | śrutaṃ deva mayā sarvaṃ rudra-yāmalasambhavam | vikṣepabhedam aśeṣeṇa sārāt sāra-vibhāgakam || 1 ||
translation: Śrī Devī said: O Lord, I have heard in full the Rudra-yāmala teaching that has arisen from the union of Rudra and Śakti, with its divisions of the manifest and the differentiated, and its distinctions from essence to essence.
intent_summary: The verse opens the dialogue by framing the text as a revelation to be clarified and distilled into its essence.
beginner_explanation: This is the beginning of a sacred conversation. The Goddess says she has heard the teaching, but wants the deepest meaning explained more clearly. It sets up the text as a search for the essential truth behind many teachings.
scholar_explanation: This opening verse situates the VBT within the broader Rudra-yāmala milieu and signals an inquiry into the sāra, the distilled essence, beyond manifold distinctions. Devi’s request anticipates the text’s movement from doctrinal plurality toward direct realization. The concern is not mere information but an existential clarification of Bhairava’s nature and means of access.

speaker: Unknown
title: Devi Questions Bhairava's True Form
sanskrit:
अद्यावप न निवृत्तो मे संशयः परमेश्वर ।
किं रूपं तत्त्वतो देि शब्दराशिकलामयम् ॥ २ ॥
transliteration: adyāpi na nivṛtto me saṃśayaḥ parameśvara | kiṃ rūpaṃ tattvato deva śabdarāśi-kalāmayam || 2 ||
translation: Even now, O Supreme Lord, my doubt has not been removed. What is your true form in reality, O God, composed of the manifold array of sounds and phases?
intent_summary: Devi asks what Bhairava really is, beyond conventional descriptions.
beginner_explanation: The Goddess is saying, “I still don’t understand.” She wants to know Bhairava’s real nature, not just a poetic description. The question points to a reality that may be beyond ordinary words.
scholar_explanation: The inquiry concerns tattvataḥ rūpa, the ontological form of Parameśvara, characterized here as śabda-rāśi-kalāmaya—an aggregate of sound and subtle phases. This links the inquiry to Tantric cosmology where vibration and articulated powers underlie manifestation. The verse anticipates the tension between spoken description and non-conceptual realization.

speaker: Unknown
title: Is Bhairava Beyond Division?
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वकं िा निात्मभेदेन भैरिे भैरिाकृतौ ।
विवशरोभेदवभन्नं िा वकं िा शविियात्मकम् ॥ ३ ॥
transliteration: kiṃ vā naivatma-bhedena bhairave bhairavākṛtau | vivasvaro-bheda-bhinnaṃ vā kiṃ vā śaktimayaṃ || 3 ||
translation: Or is it that, in Bhairava’s form as Bhairava, there is no division into self and other? Or is it divided by distinctions of radiance? Or is it constituted of Śakti?
intent_summary: The verse probes whether Bhairava is undivided consciousness, differentiated light, or pure Śakti.
beginner_explanation: She is asking whether Bhairava is one seamless reality or something made of parts and powers. She is also wondering if his nature is simply energy or light. The question keeps testing how far language can describe the absolute.
scholar_explanation: The verse stages alternatives around bheda and abheda, self-other division, and the possibility that Bhairava is śaktimaya, made of Śakti. The mention of vivasvara-bheda suggests distinctions in radiance or manifestation, but the core issue is whether Bhairava can be captured through ontic differentiation at all. The verse presses toward nondual identity while still testing symbolic mappings.

speaker: Unknown
title: Is He Inner Sound or Crowned Chakra?
sanskrit:
नादविन्दुमयं िावप वकं चन्द्राधधवनरोवधका् ।
चक्रारूढमनच्कं िा वकं िा शविस्वरूपकम् ॥ ४ ॥
transliteration: nādabindumayaṃ vāpi kiṃ candrādhonirodhikāḥ | cakrārūḍham anacakraṃ vā kiṃ vā śaktisvarūpakam || 4 ||
translation: Or is he made of sound and bindu? Or of the lunar upper and lower restraints? Or mounted on the wheel, or beyond the wheel? Or is he the very form of Śakti?
intent_summary: The verse asks whether Bhairava should be understood through subtle yogic symbols such as sound, bindu, lunar channels, and cakras.
beginner_explanation: The Goddess is naming many possible ways mystics describe reality: inner sound, a point of light, energy centers, and hidden channels. She wants to know which of these truly points to Bhairava. This shows that spiritual symbols may be signs, but not the whole truth.
scholar_explanation: The query spans nāda-bindu, lunar constriction/retention imagery, cakra symbolism, and the possibility of anacakra, beyond the psychic centers. It reflects the Tantric habit of mapping the absolute through subtle-body diagrams while questioning any final fixation on them. The closing option, śaktisvarūpa, again emphasizes the identity of Bhairava with dynamic power.

speaker: Unknown
title: Beyond Higher and Lower
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
परापरायाः सकलम् अपरायाश्च वा पुनः ।
पराया यदि तद्वत्स्यात् परत्वं तद् विरुध्यते ॥ ५ ॥
transliteration: parāparāyāḥ sakalaṃ aparāyāś ca vā punaḥ | parā yadi tadvat syāt paratvaṃ tad virudhyate || 5 ||
translation: Is he wholly of the higher and the lower, or again of the lower alone? If he were merely the higher in that way, then his supremacy would be contradicted.
intent_summary: Devi tests whether Bhairava can be reduced to categories like higher/lower or ultimate/manifest.
beginner_explanation: She is asking whether the divine can be put into neat boxes like “higher” and “lower.” Her question implies that the ultimate should not be limited by one category. If it were, it would no longer be truly supreme.
scholar_explanation: The verse interrogates parāparā and aparā distinctions central to Śākta-Tantric ontology. If the highest were merely one pole among differentiated strata, its paratva—ultimate status—would be compromised. The argument moves by negation, indicating a reality that transcends hierarchical partitioning.

speaker: Unknown
title: Beyond Parts and Bodies
sanskrit:
न हि वर्णविभेदेन देहभेदेन वा भवेत् ।
परत्वम् निष्कलत्वेन सकलत्वे न तद्भवेत् ॥ ६ ॥
transliteration: na hi varṇavibhedena dehabhedena vā bhavet | paratvam niṣkalatvena sakalatve na tad bhavet || 6 ||
translation: Supremacy cannot arise through divisions of color or through divisions of body. Because of being partless, it would not exist in the state of being composed of parts.
intent_summary: Devi concludes that the supreme cannot be defined by physical or categorical divisions.
beginner_explanation: She says the highest reality cannot be broken into pieces the way objects or bodies can. If something is truly ultimate, it must be beyond parts. This is her way of ruling out ordinary kinds of description.
scholar_explanation: The verse denies that paratva can be grounded in varṇa-bheda or deha-bheda, rejecting both chromatic and embodied differentiation as adequate accounts of the absolute. The logic of niṣkala versus sakala is crucial: the unparted cannot be coherently identified with a composite. This prepares the shift from conceptual negation to revelatory instruction.

speaker: Unknown
title: Bhavairava Praises Her Question
sanskrit:
प्रसादं कुरु मे नाथ विशेषं विवि संशयम् ।
भैरव उवाच ।
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
साधु साधु त्वया पृष्टं तन्त्रसारवमदं प्रिये ॥ ७ ॥
transliteration: prasādaṃ kuru me nātha viśeṣaṃ vivṛṇu saṃśayam | bhairava uvāca | sādhu sādhu tvayā pṛṣṭaṃ tantrasāraṃ idaṃ priye || 7 ||
translation: Show me grace, Lord, and remove my special doubt. Bhairava said: Excellent, excellent, beloved one—you have asked well; this is the essence of the Tantra.
intent_summary: Bhairava affirms the question and prepares to reveal the core teaching.
beginner_explanation: Here the teacher responds warmly and says the question is exactly right. He is about to explain the deepest heart of the teaching. The tone shifts from inquiry to revelation.
scholar_explanation: Bhairava’s response validates the query as tantrasāra, the essence of tantric instruction, and signals pedagogical readiness. The appeal to prasāda underscores grace as the condition for transmission, while viśeṣa-saṃśayam indicates a refined doubt that can now be dissolved. The verse marks the threshold between doctrinal framing and practical revelation.

speaker: Unknown
title: The Secret Teaching Is Revealed
sanskrit:
गूहनीयतमं भद्रे तथावप कथयावम ते ।
यविंवचत्सकलम् रूपम् भैरवस्य प्रकीर्तितम् ॥ ८ ॥
transliteration: gūhaṇīyatamaṃ bhadre tathāpi kathayāmi te | yad vijñeyam sakalam rūpaṃ bhairavasya prakīrtitam || 8 ||
translation: Most secret of all, O auspicious one, still I shall tell it to you. That which is to be known as the complete form of Bhairava has been proclaimed.
intent_summary: The teacher signals that the hidden essence of Bhairava will now be stated.
beginner_explanation: The teaching is said to be very secret, but the Goddess is trusted with it anyway. Bhairava says he will explain what must be known about his complete nature. This is the start of the actual instruction.
scholar_explanation: Gūhaṇīyatama emphasizes esotericism, yet the teaching is given because the interlocutor is qualified. The phrase sakalaṃ rūpam suggests the total manifested aspect of Bhairava, whose complete form will be interpreted through the dhāraṇās that follow. This verse bridges cosmological description and method.

speaker: Unknown
title: The World Is Like a Mirage
sanskrit:
तदसारतया देवि विज्ञेयं शक्रजालित् ।
मायास्वप्नोपमं चैव गन्धर्वनगरभ्रमम् ॥ ९ ॥
transliteration: tad asāratayā deve vijñeyaṃ śakrajālat | māyā-svapnopamaṃ caiva gandharva-nagara-bhramam || 9 ||
translation: O Goddess, that should be understood as insubstantial, like Indra’s net; and also like a dream of Māyā, like the भ्रम of a city of the Gandharvas.
intent_summary: The verse describes the manifested world as shimmering appearance rather than solid reality.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava says the visible world should be seen as something like a mirage or a dream. It appears real, but it is not ultimately solid. This helps the practitioner loosen their grip on appearances.
scholar_explanation: The verse deploys classic similes of appearance without substantiality: Śakra-jāla, svapna, and gandharva-nagara. These images support a non-reifying vision of manifestation, preparing the practitioner to recognize appearances as expressions of consciousness rather than independent entities. Such deconstruction is a prerequisite for nondual recognition.

speaker: Unknown
title: For Those Entangled in Conceptual Thought
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
ध्यानाथं भ्रान्तिबुद्धीनाम् वक्रयाडम्बरवर्तधनाम् ।
केवलं वर्णितं पुंसां विकल्पवनहतात्मनाम् ॥ १० ॥
transliteration: dhyānārthaṃ bhrānti-buddhīnām vakra-yāḍambara-vartinām | kevalaṃ varṇitaṃ puṃsāṃ vikalpa-vana-hātmanām || 10 ||
translation: It has been described only for men whose minds are deluded, who dwell in twisted showiness, whose very selves are lost in the forest of conceptual thought, in order to aid meditation.
intent_summary: The verse says such descriptions are provisional aids for minds trapped in concepts, not the final truth.
beginner_explanation: This means the earlier descriptions are stepping-stones, not the destination. They help people who still think in pictures and ideas begin to meditate. The goal is to go beyond mental chatter.
scholar_explanation: The verse explicitly marks the pedagogical function of upacāric description: it is dhyānārtham, a meditative support for bhrānti-buddhi and vikalpa-vana-ha. The imagery criticizes conceptual proliferation while still utilizing it as a provisional ladder. This is a standard Tantric strategy: language is employed therapeutically, then transcended.

speaker: Unknown
title: Bhairava Beyond Attributes
sanskrit:
तत्त्वतो न निजात्मासौ शब्दराशिर्न भैरवः ।
न चासौ विविधो देवो न च शक्तिसमात्मकः ॥ ११ ॥
transliteration:
tattvato na nijātmāsau śabdarāśir na bhairavaḥ |
na cāsau vividho devo na ca śaktisamātmakaḥ || 11 ||
translation: In truth, Bhairava is not merely one’s own self, nor a heap of words. He is not a god divided into many forms, nor is he identical with all the powers together.
intent_summary: To negate all limited identifications of Bhairava so the practitioner stops reducing Reality to names, forms, or concepts.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the ultimate reality cannot be pinned down as just a thought, a label, or even a particular deity-form. It is bigger than anything the mind can describe. The point is to loosen your grip on fixed ideas so you can sense what is beyond them.
scholar_explanation: The verse denies three reductions: sva-ātman as a merely personal self, śabdarāśi as a mere aggregate of words/concepts, and deva as a multiplicity of discrete divine forms. It also rejects identifying Bhairava with śakti-samātmaka, a totality of powers understood as an objectified composite. This prepares for the VBT’s apophatic method, where Bhairava is known by transcending conceptual predicates rather than by defining him.

speaker: Unknown
title: Beyond Inner Sound and Lunar Mark
sanskrit:
नादबिन्दुमयो वापि न चन्द्रार्धनिरोधिका् ।
न चक्रक्रमसम्भिन्नो न च शक्तिस्वरूपकः ॥ १२ ॥
transliteration:
nādabindumayo vāpi na candrārdhanirodhikā |
na cakrakramasambhinno na ca śaktisvarūpakaḥ || 12 ||
translation: Nor is he made of sound and bindu, nor of the lunar half-moon obstruction. He is not divided by the series of cakras, nor is he simply the form of śakti.
intent_summary: To show that even subtle yogic phenomena and internal structures are not Bhairava in their final truth.
beginner_explanation: Here the text says not to mistake inner sounds, subtle lights, or energy patterns for the whole truth. Those experiences may arise in meditation, but they are still not the ultimate reality itself. The verse helps you avoid confusing signs on the path with the destination.
scholar_explanation: This rejects identification with nāda-bindu yoga, candrārdha-nirodhikā, and cakra-krama, all of which belong to subtle-body contemplative maps. Even śakti-svarūpa is denied as a final objectification, indicating that Bhairava exceeds energetic manifestations while not being separate from them. The verse thus protects the nondual thrust of the tantra from reification of yogic experiences.

speaker: Unknown
title: This Tantra for Unprepared Minds
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अप्रिुद्धमतीनाम् वह एता िालविभीवषका् ।
मातृमोदकित्सिं प्रिृत्त्यथधमुदाहृतम् ॥ १३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
aprīuddhamatīnāṃ vahe etā ... bhayavibhīṣakāḥ |
mātṛmodakitisṃ pravṛttyartham udaghṛtam || 13 ||
translation: This Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra is spoken for those whose minds are not yet fully awakened, as a means of advancing them—like a fearful display that turns the mind toward the goal.
intent_summary: To explain that the teaching is a compassionate skillful means meant to move ordinary minds toward awakening.
beginner_explanation: The verse says this teaching is designed for people who are not yet fully clear or stable in awareness. It can feel intense or even a little frightening, but that intensity is meant to wake you up. Think of it as a strong medicine rather than a casual philosophy.
scholar_explanation: Although the OCR is corrupt, the verse clearly frames the tantra as an upāya for aprabuddha-mati, minds not yet matured into full recognition. The phrase suggests a startling or awe-inducing presentation that promotes pravṛtti toward the highest aim, rather than mere speculative discussion. This is consistent with the VBT’s didactic strategy: shocking the conceptual mind into receptivity to direct recognition.

speaker: Unknown
title: The Indescribable Absolute
sanskrit:
वदक्कालकलनोन्मुिा देशोद्देशाविशेवषणी ।
व्यपदेष्टुमशक्यासािकथ्या परमाथधत् ॥ १४ ॥
transliteration:
vaktuṃ kāla-kalanonmuktā deśoddeśaviśeṣiṇī |
vyapadeṣṭum aśakyā sā kathyā paramārthataḥ || 14 ||
translation: Free from the calculations of time, marked by no particular place or direction, it cannot truly be described; this is the supreme truth.
intent_summary: To state that ultimate reality lies beyond temporal, spatial, and linguistic specification.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the deepest reality is not located somewhere, and it is not limited by time. Because of that, ordinary language cannot fully describe it. The best you can do is point toward it and then directly experience it.
scholar_explanation: The text negates kāla-kalana, deśa, and uddeśa, thereby removing temporal and spatial predicates from paramārtha. Since the Absolute is beyond designation (vyapadeśa), it is approached through direct insight rather than discursive reference. This sets the stage for the verse’s later movement from theology into meditative praxis.

speaker: Unknown
title: The Bhairavi State of Self-Experience
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अन्त् स्वानुभिानन्दा विकल्पोन्मुिगोचरा ।
यािस्था भवरताकारा भैरिी भैरिात्मन् ॥ १५ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
antar svānubhavānandā vikalponmuktagocharā |
yāvasthā bhairatākārā bhairavī bhairavātman || 15 ||
translation: The condition that is inwardly the bliss of one’s own direct experience, free from conceptual thought, and whose nature is Bhairava-like—this is Bhairavi, the very essence of Bhairava.
intent_summary: To identify the supreme state as inward, self-luminous bliss beyond conceptualization and as the feminine face of Bhairava-consciousness.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a state where awareness is inwardly bright, joyful, and free from constant mental chatter. It is not something you think about; it is something you directly taste. The text says this is Bhairavi, the living power of Bhairava himself.
scholar_explanation: Here svānubhava-ananda names the immediate bliss of self-recognition, while vikalpa-unmukta marks freedom from conceptual proliferation. The phrase bhairatākārā/bhairavī indicates the same nondual reality viewed as śakti, the dynamic mode of awareness. This is a key doctrine of the tantra: Bhairava and Bhairavī are not two, but one reality in complementary aspect.

speaker: Unknown
title: Worship Nothing Beyond That
sanskrit:
तद्वपुस्तत्त्वतो ज्ञेयं विमलं विश्वपूरणम् ।
एिं विधे परे तत्त्वे क् पूज्य् कश्च तृप्यवत ॥ १६ ॥
transliteration:
tad vapuḥ tattvato jñeyaṃ vimalam viśvapūraṇam |
evaṃ vidhe pare tattve kaḥ pūjyaḥ kaś ca tṛpyati || 16 ||
translation: That form is to be known in truth as pure and pervading the universe. In such a supreme principle, who is there to worship, and who is there to be satisfied?
intent_summary: To dissolve the sense of a separate worshipper and an external object of worship in the recognition of all-pervading reality.
beginner_explanation: If everything is already filled by that pure awareness, then there is no separate thing standing outside it to be worshipped. There is also no separate person left who could be “satisfied” by an external object. The verse pushes you toward a direct, whole-body recognition of unity.
scholar_explanation: The verse defines the vapuḥ of that state as vimala and viśva-pūraṇa, pure and cosmos-pervading, and then draws the logical consequence: in such a param tattva, dualistic pūjā collapses. The worshipper, the worshipped, and the act of worship lose their separateness. This is a classic nondual ritual reversal in Śaiva tantra.

speaker: Unknown
title: Supreme Bhairavi Defined
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
एिं विधा भैरिस्य यािस्था पवरगीयते ।
सा परा पररूपेण परा देिी प्रकीवतधता ॥ १७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava tantram |
evaṃ vidho bhairavasya yāvasthā parigīyate |
sā parā pararūpeṇa parā devī prakīrtitā || 17 ||
translation: The condition of Bhairava that is praised in this way is proclaimed as the Supreme Goddess, who is supreme by virtue of her transcendent form.
intent_summary: To state that Bhairava’s realized state is inseparable from the Supreme Goddess, the transcendent dynamic of awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the highest state of Bhairava is also called the Supreme Goddess. In other words, the still, awakened awareness and its living power are not two different things. It is one reality spoken of in two ways.
scholar_explanation: The verse equates the praised bhairava-avasthā with parā devī, emphasizing parā as both supreme and transcendentally manifest (pararūpeṇa). This supports the nondual śiva-śakti identity central to Trika: awareness and its power are distinguishable only conceptually. The formulation also links mystical realization with theological personification.

speaker: Unknown
title: Always Abiding as Śakti
sanskrit:
शविशविमतोयधद्वद् अभेद् सिधदा वस्थत् ।
अतस्तद्धमधवमधत्वात् पराशवि् परात्मन् ॥ १८ ॥
transliteration:
śivaśaktimato yadvad abhedaḥ sarvadā sthitaḥ |
atas taddharmadharmatvāt parāśaktiḥ parātman || 18 ||
translation: Just as Śiva and Śakti are always established as non-different, so from the nature of that principle as bearer of its own qualities, it is the Supreme Power, the Supreme Self.
intent_summary: To affirm the inseparability of Śiva and Śakti as the philosophical basis for realizing the Supreme Self.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that Śiva and Śakti are never truly separate. They are two ways of talking about the same living reality: still awareness and its active power. Recognizing that unity helps you see your own deepest self as more than a separate ego.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes the perennial abheda of śiva-śakti, grounded in dharma-dharmitva: a principle and its qualities are not separate. Consequently, parāśakti and parātman are co-referential expressions of the same ultimate reality. This is foundational Trika metaphysics, where manifestation is not a fall from awareness but its intrinsic self-expression.

speaker: Unknown
title: Entering the Knowledge State
sanskrit:
न िह्नेदाधवहका शविव्यधवतवरिा विभाव्यते ।
केिलम् ज्ञानसत्तायां प्रारम्भोऽयं प्रिेशने ॥ १९ ॥
transliteration:
na vahned ārdhāhavāka śaktir vyatiriktā vibhāvyate |
kevalam jñāna-sattāyāṃ prārambho ’yaṃ praveśane || 19 ||
translation: The power is not to be imagined as something separate from the fire of knowledge. This is only the beginning of entry into the state of pure knowing.
intent_summary: To direct the practitioner to understand power as inseparable from awareness and to treat the teaching as an initial doorway into realization.
beginner_explanation: The verse says you should not imagine spiritual power as something separate from awareness, like heat separate from fire. The real point is to enter a state of clear knowing, not to collect special experiences. So this is an opening step, not the final destination.
scholar_explanation: The OCR is unstable, but the sense is that śakti is not to be posited as vyatirikta from the jñāna-agni. Instead, the verse marks a prārambha toward jñāna-sattā, the ontological condition of knowing as being. This resonates with the VBT’s pedagogy: techniques are doorways into recognition, not independent metaphysical entities.

speaker: Unknown
title: Absorption into Śakti-State
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
शक्त्यिस्थाप्रविष्टस्य वनविधभागेन भािना ।
तदासौ वशिरूपी स्यात् शैिी मुखवमहोच्यते ॥ २० ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava tantram |
śaktyavasthāpraviṣṭasya nirvibhāgena bhāvanā |
tadāsau śivarūpī syāt śaivī mukham ihocyate || 20 ||
translation: For one who has entered the state of Śakti, contemplation without division is employed. Then that one becomes of the form of Śiva; this is called the Śaiva face here.
intent_summary: To instruct the practitioner to enter the energy-state and contemplate without dividing subject and object until Śiva-nature is recognized.
beginner_explanation: This verse describes a meditation where you settle fully into the living energy of experience and stop splitting things into “me” and “that.” When that division disappears, you recognize yourself as Śiva. It is like seeing the wave as not other than the ocean.
scholar_explanation: The phrase śaktyavasthā-praviṣṭa indicates immersion in the dynamic aspect of consciousness, while nirvibhāgena bhāvanā specifies nondual contemplation free of conceptual segmentation. The result is śivarūpī, a recognition of one’s form as Śiva, described as the śaivī mukha or face of the tradition. This is a paradigmatic VBT transition from entry into śakti to realization of identity with Śiva.

speaker: Unknown
title: Knowledge Through Difference and Non-Difference
sanskrit:
यथालोकेन दीपस्य वकरणैभाधस्करस्य च ।
ज्ञायते वदवविभागावद तद्वच्छक्त्या वशि् वप्रये ॥ २१ ॥
transliteration:
yathā lokena dīpasya vakraṇair bhāskarasya ca |
jñāyate veda-vibhāgāvād tadvat śaktyā vaśi priyé || 21 ||
translation: As through a lamp and the sun their differences are known, so, beloved, by Śakti the distinctions of the knowable are known.
intent_summary: It teaches that differentiated knowing arises through the power of consciousness itself.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that we recognize things by the light of awareness, just as a lamp helps reveal objects and the sun reveals the world. In the same way, all knowledge is possible because consciousness illuminates everything. The point is to notice the awareness behind every act of knowing.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses the lamp and sun as analogies for vyavahāra-jñāna, the ordinary discrimination by which distinctions are apprehended. Śakti is not merely an external power but the self-revealing capacity of consciousness (cit-śakti), without which even veda/vibhāga would remain unmanifest. This prepares the shift from conceptual knowing to direct recognition of Bhairava as the source of all cognition.

speaker: Unknown
title: Devi Questions Bhairava Beyond Time and Space
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
श्री देव्युवाच ।
देिदेि विशूलाङ्क कपालकृतभूषण ।
वदवदेशकालशून्या च व्यपदेशवििवजधता ॥ २२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava-tantram |
śrī devy uvāca |
deva deva viśālākṣa kapālakṛta-bhūṣaṇa |
deśa-kāla-śūnyā ca vyapadeśa-vivarjhitā || 22 ||
translation: The Goddess said: O God of gods, wide-eyed one, adorned with a garland of skulls, you are beyond place and time and free from all designation.
intent_summary: It frames Devi’s recognition that Bhairava transcends all spatiotemporal categories and names.
beginner_explanation: Here the Goddess addresses Bhairava and says he is beyond ordinary ideas like here and there, now and later. She is acknowledging that true reality cannot be pinned down by labels or locations. This sets up her request for a direct way to realize him.
scholar_explanation: Devi identifies Bhairava as deśa-kāla-śūnya and vyapadeśa-vivarjita, indicating transcendence of all limiting predicates. The epithet kapālakṛta-bhūṣaṇa points to the iconography of Bhairava, but the doctrinal emphasis is on the unconditioned nature of consciousness beyond kalpanā and designation. This is a formal transition from ontological praise to sādhana inquiry.

speaker: Unknown
title: Devi Asks for the Direct Way to Bhairava
sanskrit:
यािस्था भवरताकारा भैरवस्योपलभ्यते ।
कैरुपायैर्मुखम् तस्य परा देवि कथं भवेत् ।
यथा सम्यगहम् देवि तथा मे ब्रूवह भैरव ॥ २३ ॥
transliteration:
yāvasthā bhairavākārā bhairavasya upalabhyate |
kair upāyair mukham tasya parā devi kathaṃ bhavet |
yathā samyag ahaṃ devi tathā me brūhi bhairava || 23 ||
translation: In what state is Bhairava’s form apprehended? By what means, O supreme Goddess, does one reach his face? Bhairava, tell me truly just as it is.
intent_summary: It asks for the practical method by which Bhairava’s nature can be directly realized.
beginner_explanation: The Goddess is asking for a method, not just an idea. She wants to know what state of mind or practice lets someone directly meet Bhairava. This question opens the doorway to the meditation techniques that follow.
scholar_explanation: The verse asks in what avasthā Bhairavākāra is upalabhyate and by what upāya his mukha or presence is attained. Mukha here implies direct encounter or access, not merely visual image, and the request anticipates the 112 dhāraṇās as embodied means of recognition. The urgency of samyag brūhi emphasizes exact transmission of the upāya rather than speculative doctrine.

speaker: Unknown
title: Upward Breath and Lower Life Force
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
श्री भैरव उवाच ।
ऊर्ध्वे प्राणो ह्यधो जीवो विसर्गात्मा परोच्चरेत् ।
उत्पत्तिविधयस्थाने भरणाद्भवता स्थिति् ॥ २४ ॥
transliteration:
ūrdhve prāṇo hy adho jīvo visargātmā paroccaret |
utpatti-vidhaya-sthāne bharaṇād bhavataḥ sthitiḥ || 24 ||
translation: The prāṇa moves upward, the jīva downward; the essence of emission rises beyond. By filling at the place of arising and dissolution, there is abiding in your state.
intent_summary: It teaches meditation on the movement and pause of breath to enter Bhairava’s stable presence.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to paying attention to the breath’s movement upward and downward. By noticing the natural pause and fullness at the turning point, the mind can settle into a deeper stillness. That stillness is presented as a doorway to a more universal state of being.
scholar_explanation: Prāṇa and jīva are here contrasted as ascending and descending dynamics, while visargātmā suggests the released or emanative essence that can be transmuted into realization. Utpatti and sthiti denote the thresholds of emergence and sustaining, and bharaṇa indicates full absorption into the interval where breath is held or naturally suspended. This is a classic kumbhaka-based dhāraṇā linking physiological transition to Bhairava-sthiti.

speaker: Unknown
title: Bhairava Revealed in the Meeting of Opposites
sanskrit:
मरुतोऽन्तर्हविः वा वियद्युमावनितधनात् ।
भैरव्या भैरवस्येत्थं भैरवि व्यज्यते वपुः ॥ २५ ॥
transliteration:
maruto 'ntar havir vā viyad-ādy-avamāna-dhanāt |
bhairavyā bhairavasyaitthaṃ bhairavi vyajyate vapuḥ || 25 ||
translation: In the inward offering of the winds, or in the treasury of sky and the like, O Bhairavi, thus is Bhairava’s body revealed.
intent_summary: It indicates that Bhairava is disclosed when opposites and elemental contents are inwardly unified.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that Bhairava can be recognized in subtle inner experience, not just in outer forms. Images of breath, space, and inward offering all point to a deeper unity. The practice is to look for the sacred presence inside ordinary experience.
scholar_explanation: Marutaḥ and haviḥ evoke prāṇic currents and inner oblation, while viyad and related terms point to the subtle spatial field of consciousness. The verse suggests that Bhairava’s vapuḥ becomes manifest not in external objectification but in the inward sacrificial integration of forces. It is a non-dual sacramental vision where the body of Bhairava is the totality of lived experience when seen as śakti-play.

speaker: Unknown
title: Middle State Beyond Going and Entering
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
न व्रजेन्न विशेच्छविमधरुद्रूपा विकावसते ।
वनविधकल्पतया मध्ये तया भैरिरूपता ॥ २६ ॥
transliteration:
na vrajen na viśec chāvi madhya-rūpā vikāśate |
na vihanyeta kalpataḥ madhye tayā bhairavī-rūpatā || 26 ||
translation: Neither going out nor entering in, in the middle form shines forth. Not through conceptual construction is it injured; in the middle, by that, the form of Bhairavī appears.
intent_summary: It teaches resting in the middle condition where awareness is free from movement and thought-construction.
beginner_explanation: This verse says not to chase thoughts outward or sink into them inward. Instead, there is a middle state that simply shines by itself. If you stay there, you may sense a quiet, luminous presence.
scholar_explanation: The central term madhya-rūpā points to the in-between or non-polarized condition, a frequent VBT locus of realization. Na vrajet / na viśet negates both outward projection and inward withdrawal, while kalpanā is explicitly rejected as the means of access. Bhairavī-rūpatā arises when awareness abides in the nondual middle that is untouched by conceptual modification.

speaker: Unknown
title: Peace at the End of the Breath Cycle
sanskrit:
कुवम्भता रेवचता िावप पूर्वता िा यदा भिेत् ।
तदन्ते शान्तनामासौ शक्त्या शान्त् प्रकाशते ॥ २७ ॥
transliteration:
kumbhatā revatā vāpi pūrvatā vā yadā bhavet |
tad ante śānta-nāmāsau śaktyā śāntaḥ prakāśate || 27 ||
translation: When the breath is held, or when it moves out or in, at the end of that, the one called Peace shines forth, peaceful through Śakti.
intent_summary: It teaches observing the end of breath movement as a doorway to peaceful awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse focuses on the moments when breathing stops briefly after inhaling, exhaling, or holding. Those tiny pauses are special because the mind can become quiet there. The teaching is to notice that peaceful gap and stay with it.
scholar_explanation: The three possible conditions—kumbhatā, recakatā, and pūrvatā—indicate the breath-phase transitions where śānta-nāma becomes manifest. The emphasis is not merely on restraint but on the revealed peace that shines by śakti at the end of movement. This is a practical entry into the VBT’s recurring use of sandhi, the junction, as a site of recognition.

speaker: Unknown
title: Contemplate the Subtle Flame at the Root
sanskrit:
आमूलाविरणाभासां सूक्ष्मात् सूक्ष्मतरावत्मकाम् ।
वचन्तयेत्ताम् वद्वषट्कान्ते श्याम्यन्तीम् भैरवोदयः ॥ २८ ॥
transliteration:
āmūlāvirabhāsāṃ sūkṣmāt sūkṣmatarātmikām |
cintayet tāṃ dvādaśānte śāmyantīṃ bhairavodayaḥ || 28 ||
translation: One should contemplate that luminous subtle one, subtler than the subtle, at the root radiance; at the end of the twelve, as it subsides, Bhairava arises.
intent_summary: It instructs meditation on a subtle inner light or radiance until it dissolves into Bhairava-awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse invites you to picture or sense a very subtle light, even finer than anything physical. As you keep attention there, the light settles and quiets down. In that quieting, a deeper awareness emerges.
scholar_explanation: Āmūla-āvirabhāsāṃ indicates a root-level radiance, perhaps the kuṇḍalinī or inner jyotis, while dvādaśānta refers to the classical subtle point at the crown or twelve-finger measure beyond the body. The act of cintana is not mere imagination but stable contemplative fixation on the subtle luminous field until śamya and bhairavodaya coincide. The verse integrates visualization with dissolution into nondual awareness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Lightning-Like Rising Through the Centers
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
उद्गच्छन्तं तवडद्रूपाम् प्रवतचक्रं क्रमात्क्रमम् ।
ऊर्ध्वं मुवष्टियं याित् तािदन्ते महोदय् ॥ २९ ॥
transliteration:
udgacchantaṃ tārad-rūpam pravicakraṃ kramāt kramam |
ūrdhvaṃ muṣṭiṃ yāñt tad ante mahodayam || 29 ||
translation: The lightning-like form rising, passing through the centers step by step, when the fist ascends upward, at that end there is great awakening.
intent_summary: It teaches visualizing a rising luminous movement through subtle centers to trigger awakening.
beginner_explanation: This verse describes attention moving like a flash of lightning upward through the body. You follow that rising energy step by step, almost like tracking a spark. At the top of the movement, there is a powerful opening or awakening.
scholar_explanation: The tārad-rūpa imagery suggests a rapid luminous ascent, often read as śakti moving through cakra-like loci or subtle centers. Pravicakraṃ and kramāt kramam emphasize ordered progression rather than random visualization, while ūrdhvaṃ muṣṭiṃ is an obscure but likely somatic gesture or upward containment. The culmination is mahodaya, a great arising of consciousness beyond ordinary embodiment.

speaker: Unknown
title: Twelvefold Method Across Gross and Subtle
sanskrit:
क्रमद्वादशकं सम्यग् द्वादशाक्षरभेवदतम् ।
स्थूलसूक्ष्मपरवस्थत्या मुक्त्वा मुक्त्वान्तत् वशि् ॥ ३० ॥
transliteration:
kramadvādaśakaṃ samyag dvādaśākṣarabhāvitam |
sthūla-sūkṣma-parāvasthātyā muktvā muktvāntataḥ śivaḥ || 30 ||
translation: The twelvefold क्रम should be perfectly practiced, contemplated through the twelve-syllabled [mantra]; by freeing from the gross, the subtle, and the supreme states, one is finally liberated into Śiva.
intent_summary: It teaches mantra-linked progression through layers of experience until all states are transcended.
beginner_explanation: This verse says to work with a twelve-step or twelve-part method, often tied to a sacred mantra. The practice helps you loosen your grip on the body, then subtler feelings, and even refined states of meditation. In the end, what remains is a freedom described as Śiva.
scholar_explanation: Kramadvādaśaka evokes a structured sequence, likely related to the twelve-syllable mantra and its meditative deployment. The verse explicitly names sthūla, sūkṣma, and parā avasthā as domains to be relinquished, indicating a layered transcendence rather than one-dimensional absorption. Muktvā muktvā emphasizes successive release culminating in identity with Śiva, consistent with the nondual telos of the text.

speaker: Unknown
title: Breath Rising Through the Crown
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
तयापूयाधशु मूर्धान्तं भङ्क्त्वा भ्रूक्षेपसेतुना ।
वनविधकल्पं मन् कृत्वा सिरूर्ध्वे सिधगोद्गम् ॥ ३१ ॥
transliteration:
tayā pūrvyārdhaśu mūrdhāntaṃ bhaṅktvā bhṛkṣepasetu nā |
vanavidhikalpaṃ man kṛtvā sirūrdhve sidhagodgam || 31 ||
translation: Breaking through the crown at the top of the head by means of the bridge of the eyebrow-movement, and making the mind into the form of a forest of thoughts, one rises upward to the state of perfection.
intent_summary: Use an upward inner gesture linked to the brows and crown to break through limitation and lift awareness into a higher state.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a subtle practice of directing attention upward, especially through the space between the eyebrows and the top of the head. The imagery is unusual, but the basic idea is to use a focused inner lift to move beyond ordinary thinking. Think of it as raising your attention like a beam of light through the top of the head.
scholar_explanation: The verse appears to describe a contemplative ascent through the mūrdhānta, using bhṛkṣepa or a brow-directed inner motion as a ‘bridge’ (setu) to pierce the upper aperture. The mind is intentionally shaped into a particular mode and then transcended, culminating in siddhi or an elevated realization. This belongs with other VBT techniques that use anatomical focal points as supports for śūnya or higher absorption.

speaker: Unknown
title: Contemplating the Five Emptinesses
sanskrit:
वशवखपक्षैवश्चिरूपैमण्डलै् शून्यपञ्चकम् ।
ध्यायतोऽनुत्तरे शून्ये प्रिेशो हृदये भिेत् ॥ ३२ ॥
transliteration:
vaśavakṣapaṅkṣaivaś cirūpair maṇḍalaiḥ śūnya-pañcakam |
dhyāyato'nuttare śūnye prāveśo hṛdaye bhavet || 32 ||
translation: By contemplating the five emptinesses with the forms of the wheels, wings, and other shapes, there comes entry into the heart through the unsurpassed void.
intent_summary: Meditate on structured forms as gateways into the heart of boundless emptiness.
beginner_explanation: Here the text asks you to contemplate the idea of emptiness in a very deliberate way, using visual patterns or symbolic shapes as supports. The goal is not to get lost in the images, but to let them lead you into a vast inner openness. That openness is said to open directly in the heart.
scholar_explanation: The verse likely refers to the pañca-śūnya, the five voids or fivefold inner spaces, mediated by maṇḍala-like forms. The ‘unutterable void’ (anuttara-śūnya) is not mere blankness but the supreme openness of consciousness. Entry into the hṛdaya indicates realization of the central locus where awareness rests in nondual fullness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Spontaneous Merging into the Void
sanskrit:
ईदृशेन क्रमेणैि यि कुिावप वचन्तना ।
शून्ये कुड्ये परे पािे स्वयम् लीना िरप्रदा ॥ ३३ ॥
transliteration:
īdṛśena krameṇaiva yad kuṭāv api vācintanā |
śūnye kuḍye pare pāve svayam līnā vara-pradā || 33 ||
translation: By this method, even whatever thought arises in a hut or elsewhere becomes, of itself, dissolved in the void, and grants the boon of the supreme.
intent_summary: Let all thoughts dissolve on their own into openness, so that the highest blessing appears naturally.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that if you practice this way, even ordinary thoughts in any setting can melt into emptiness by themselves. You do not need to force them away. When they disappear on their own, the mind becomes free and something greater can shine through.
scholar_explanation: The emphasis is on effortless laya: thoughts (vācintanā) generated in any place or condition are absorbed into śūnya without coercion. The ‘supreme’ (para) is the nondual ground that confers vara-pradā, the ‘boon-giving’ power of realization. This verse underscores the portability of the practice: the locus is not external circumstance but the inner absorption into śūnya.

speaker: Unknown
title: Fixing the Gaze on the Crown
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
कपालान्तमधनो न्यस्य वतष्ठन्मीवलतलोचन् ।
क्रमेण मनसो दार्ढ्यात् लक्षयेत् लक्ष्यं उत्तमम् ॥ ३४ ॥
transliteration:
kapālāntam adho nyasya tiṣṭhan mīlitalocan |
krameṇa manaso dārḍhyāt lakṣayet lakṣyam uttamam || 34 ||
translation: Placing the skull-aperture below, and standing with the eyes closed, one should, through the firmness of mind, gradually aim at the supreme target.
intent_summary: Close the eyes, steady the mind, and focus on the highest inner aim beyond ordinary sight.
beginner_explanation: This verse describes a simple but powerful kind of inner focusing. You close your eyes, settle the body, and keep your mind steady on a deeper target rather than on external objects. The practice is about concentration becoming strong enough to point beyond the usual world.
scholar_explanation: The imagery of kapālānta suggests awareness oriented around the cranial aperture or upper interior threshold, with mīlitalocana indicating withdrawal from external vision. By manaso dārḍhya, the practitioner stabilizes attention until the uttama lakṣya is intuited. This is a classical dhāraṇā of sustained concentration leading to transphysical seeing.

speaker: Unknown
title: Awareness in the Middle Channel
sanskrit:
मध्यनाडी मध्यसंस्था विससूत्राभरूपया ।
ध्यातान्तव्योमया देव्या तया देवि प्रकाशते ॥ ३५ ॥
transliteration:
madhyanāḍī madhyasaṃsthā viśvasūtrābhirūpayā |
dhyānāntavyomayā devyā tayā devi prakāśate || 35 ||
translation: The Goddess shines forth through that which is situated in the middle channel, beautiful like the thread of the world, and consisting of the inner sky of meditation.
intent_summary: Rest attention in the central channel and inner space so that the luminous Goddess reveals herself.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to the subtle center of the body, often imagined as a channel running up the middle. When attention rests there, it becomes like looking into an inner sky. In that stillness, the deepest presence is said to reveal itself.
scholar_explanation: The madhyanāḍī is the central suṣumnā-like pathway, identified with the viśvasūtra, the ‘thread of the universe.’ The deity appears as dhyānāntavyoma, the inner sky of meditation, showing that awareness itself is the luminous medium of manifestation. This is a key nondual Tantric move: the Goddess is not elsewhere but shines through the centered awareness of the practitioner.

speaker: Unknown
title: Gaze Through the Brow Gate
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
कररुद्धदृगस्त्रेण भ्रूभेदाद्द्वाररोधनात् ।
दृष्टे विन्दौ क्रमाल्लीने तन्मध्ये परमा वस्थवत् ॥ ३६ ॥
transliteration:
kararuddhadṛgastreṇa bhūrbhedād dvārarodhanāt |
dṛṣṭe bindau kramāl līne tanmadhye paramā vasthitiḥ || 36 ||
translation: By means of the weapon of vision held back with the hands, by piercing the brow and blocking the door, when the bindu is seen and gradually dissolved, there is the supreme state in the middle of that.
intent_summary: Use a closed, inward gaze at the brow to enter the bindu and dissolve into the highest stillness.
beginner_explanation: This verse suggests gently covering or restraining the eyes and directing attention to the space at the brow. As the focus becomes steady, a small point of light or presence may appear. By staying with it, attention can dissolve into a deeper stillness.
scholar_explanation: The practice combines bodily restraint (kararuddha-dṛk) with attention to the bhūrbheda, the piercing of the brow center. The bindu is then perceived and progressively absorbed (kramāl līna), revealing the paramāvasthiti located ‘in the middle,’ a recurring VBT motif for nondual realization. The ‘weapon’ metaphor indicates precision: concentrated seeing that cuts through ordinary perception.

speaker: Unknown
title: Dissolving the Point of Light
sanskrit:
धामान्त् क्षोभसम्भूतसूक्ष्माविवतलकाकृवतम् ।
विन्दुं वशखान्ते हृदये लयान्ते ध्यायतो लय् ॥ ३७ ॥
transliteration:
dhāmāntakṣobhasambhūta-sūkṣmāvitalakākṛtim |
binduṃ viśikhānte hṛdaye layānte dhyāyato layaḥ || 37 ||
translation: Meditating on the bindu, a subtle form like a streak of lightning arising from the vibration at the end of the path of light, one attains dissolution in the heart at the end of dissolution.
intent_summary: Contemplate the subtle light-point until it dissolves into the heart’s final absorption.
beginner_explanation: This verse speaks of noticing a tiny flash or point of light that appears in deep meditation. You stay with it without forcing anything, and it naturally fades into a deeper inner quiet. The ending point is not loss, but absorption into the heart.
scholar_explanation: The bindu here is linked with a subtle luminous trace (sūkṣmāvitāla-kākṛti) arising from dhāmānta-kṣobha, the trembling at the limit of luminosity or perception. The verse culminates in laya in the hṛdaya, showing the heart as the locus where luminosity reabsorbs into the source. This is a subtle inversion of manifestation: the light-point leads back to its own dissolution.

speaker: Unknown
title: Entering the Unstruck Sound
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अनाहते पािकणेऽभिशब्दे सवरद्द्रुते ।
शब्दब्रह्मवण वनष्णात् परं ब्रह्मावधगच्छवत ॥ ३८ ॥
transliteration:
anāhate pāvakale 'bhiśabde svarad drute |
śabdabrahmaṇi niṣṇātaḥ paraṃ brahmādhigacchati || 38 ||
translation: In the unstruck sound, in the swiftly moving inner sound, one skilled in the sound-brahman attains the supreme Brahman.
intent_summary: Listen inwardly to the subtle sound current until it leads beyond sound into ultimate reality.
beginner_explanation: This verse is about hearing a very subtle inner sound that does not come from outside. Instead of listening with your ears, you listen inwardly and follow the sound as it changes. By becoming familiar with that inner resonance, you can go beyond it to a deeper silence.
scholar_explanation: Anāhata refers to the unstruck, spontaneously arising inner sound, a classic nāda-yoga support. The practitioner who is niṣṇāta in śabdabrahman, the sonic absolute, transcends even that medium and realizes paraṃ brahma. The sound is not the goal but a vehicle from gross vibration to nondual consciousness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Repeating AUM into Emptiness
sanskrit:
प्रणिावदसमुच्चारात् प्लुतान्ते शून्यभािानात् ।
शून्यया परया शक्त्या शून्यतामेवत भैरवि ॥ ३९ ॥
transliteration:
praṇavādisamuccārāt plutānte śūnyabhāvanāt |
śūnyayā parayā śaktyā śūnyatām eti bhairavi || 39 ||
translation: Through the utterance of praṇava and the like, and by contemplating emptiness at the end of the extended sound, O Bhairavī, one reaches emptiness by means of the supreme power of emptiness.
intent_summary: Use mantra sound, especially AUM, to dissolve into the silent gap and the power of emptiness.
beginner_explanation: This verse teaches a very simple practice: say a sacred sound like AUM slowly, and pay attention to the quiet at the end. That quiet is not dead space; it is full of presence. By resting there, you enter a deeper openness.
scholar_explanation: The verse combines praṇava-japa with plutānta, the extended end of the sound, to trigger śūnyabhāvanā. Śūnyā parā śakti is the supreme power of emptiness, indicating that voidness is not absence but the dynamic potency of consciousness. This is a canonical VBT method: mantra culminates in silence and the practitioner enters śūnyatā.

speaker: Unknown
title: Becoming the Form of Emptiness
sanskrit:
यस्य कस्यावप िणधस्य पूिाधन्तािनुभाियेत् ।
शून्यया शून्यभूतोऽसौ शून्याकार् पुमान्भिेत् ॥ ४० ॥
transliteration:
yasyakasyāpi varṇasya pūrvāntāvanubhāvayet |
śūnyayā śūnyabhūto'sau śūnyākāraḥ pumān bhavet || 40 ||
translation: By contemplating the beginning and end of any letter whatsoever, one becomes empty by means of emptiness, and that person becomes of the form of emptiness.
intent_summary: Use any sound or letter as a doorway to perceive its arising and ending, then rest as empty awareness itself.
beginner_explanation: This verse says you can work with any letter or sound, not just a special mantra. Watch how it begins and ends, and notice the space around it. If you stay with that space, your mind becomes quiet and open.
scholar_explanation: The contemplative move is to observe the pūrvānta and, by implication, the ending of any varṇa, revealing their dependence on śūnya. The result is śūnyabhūta, a subject transformed into the form of emptiness, which is an experiential nonduality rather than mere negation. The verse generalizes the mantra practice into a universal phonological dhāraṇā.

speaker: Unknown
title: Awareness at the End of Sound
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
तन्त्र्यावदिाद्यशब्देषु दीघेषु क्रमसवम्स्थते् ।
अनन्यचेता् प्रत्यन्ते परव्योमिपुभधिेत् ॥ ४१ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava-tantram |
trantriyāvadiādyaśabdeṣu dīrgheṣu kramasaṃsthite |
ananyacetāḥ pratyante paravyomnipubha dhayet || 41 ||
translation: In the long, successive sounds of a string or similar instrument, when the mind is fixed without distraction, one should meditate on the supreme space (paravyoman) at the end [of the sound].
intent_summary: Use the tail-end of sustained sound as a doorway into the vast stillness beyond sound.
beginner_explanation: Listen to a long musical note or continuous sound, and pay special attention to the moment it fades away. Instead of following the sound itself, rest in the quiet that remains when it ends. That silence can open into a sense of spacious awareness.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā uses the sonic continuum of long notes and their terminal fade as a support for entering paravyoman, the transcendental “supreme space.” The key move is ananyacetas, undistracted one-pointedness, at the anta or pratyante of sound, where vibration resolves into stillness. It reflects a classic Tantric use of nāda as a bridge from gross perception to subtle awareness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Mantra Dissolving into Void
sanskrit:
वपण्डमन्त्रस्य सिधस्य स्थूलिणधक्रमेण तु ।
अधेन्दुविन्दुनादान्त् शून्योच्चाराद्भिेवच्छि् ॥ ४२ ॥
transliteration:
piṇḍamantrasya sidhasya sthūlapiṇḍakrameṇa tu |
adha-indu-bindu-nādāntān śūnyoccārād bhaved dhruvam || 42 ||
translation: For a perfected mantra embodied in a gross, articulated form, by proceeding through the lower moon, bindu, and nāda, one surely attains the fixed state through utterance of śūnya, the void.
intent_summary: Follow the mantra inward through subtler and subtler phases until it dissolves into emptiness.
beginner_explanation: A mantra is not just a sound; it can be traced inward to quieter and subtler levels. This verse says to move past the obvious sound into finer phases and finally into stillness and emptiness. At the end, the mantra becomes a doorway to silence, not just a spoken phrase.
scholar_explanation: The verse describes the internal ascent/descent of a siddha mantra through sthūla articulation toward adhaḥ-indu, bindu, and nāda, culminating in śūnyoccāra, an utterance of void. This is a mantra-laya practice in which phonation becomes progressively subtle until the practitioner stabilizes in dhruva, the fixed contemplative state. The imagery matches Tantric phonology where sound unfolds from gross speech to undifferentiated silence.

speaker: Unknown
title: Identity with Universal Space
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
वनजदेहे सिधवदक्कम् युगपद्भाियेवद्वयत् ।
वनविधकल्पमनास्तस्य वियत्सिधम् प्रितधते ॥ ४३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava-tantram |
svadehe siddhavad ekatvaṃ yugapad bhāvayed dvayam |
nirvikalpa-manās tasya viyat-siddhiṃ prapadyate || 43 ||
translation: In one's own body, one should simultaneously contemplate unity as if it were already accomplished, while [also] contemplating duality; for one whose mind is free of conceptualization, the attainment of space (viyat-siddhi) arises.
intent_summary: Hold body and world together without division until the mind opens into the realization of space-consciousness.
beginner_explanation: This practice asks you to look at your own body while also sensing the wider field around it, without separating “inside” from “outside.” If you can keep the mind simple and not keep labeling everything, a feeling of open space can emerge. The goal is not to think harder, but to relax into a bigger way of being.
scholar_explanation: Here the sādhaka contemplates ekatva and dvaya simultaneously within svadeha, until nirvikalpa-manas dissolves the constructed split and viyat-siddhi appears. The verse is not advocating logical contradiction but a Tantric superimposition that destabilizes subject-object fixation, revealing space as an aspect of Bhairava-consciousness. This aligns with VBT’s frequent move of using perceptual paradox to trigger nondual recognition.

speaker: Unknown
title: Void of Back and Root
sanskrit:
पृष्टशून्यम् मूलशून्यम् युगपद्भाियेच्च य् ।
शरीरवनरपेवक्षण्या शक्त्या शून्यमना भिेत् ॥ ४४ ॥
transliteration:
pṛṣṭha-śūnyaṃ mūla-śūnyaṃ yugapad bhāvayecca yaḥ |
śarīra-nirapekṣā yā śaktyā śūnya-mano bhavet || 44 ||
translation: One who simultaneously contemplates the void of the back and the void of the root becomes a mind of emptiness through the power that is independent of the body.
intent_summary: Use bodily voids and inner energy to let the mind become spacious and empty.
beginner_explanation: Feel the open space behind your back and the open space at the base of the body at the same time. Don’t strain to imagine anything; just let the body feel hollow and open. As this grows, the mind can become quiet and spacious on its own.
scholar_explanation: The verse directs attention to pṛṣṭha-śūnya and mūla-śūnya, two bodily loci used as contemplative voids, simultaneously. The resulting śūnya-manas is not mere blankness but a state generated by śarīra-nirapekṣā śakti, the power not dependent on gross embodiment. This is a body-based entry into śūnya that prepares for recognition of the subtle power underlying sensation and space.

speaker: Unknown
title: Heart Void and Instantaneous Emptying
sanskrit:
पृष्टशून्यं मूलशून्यं हृच्छून्यं भाियेविरम् ।
युगपवन्नविधकल्पत्वावन्नविधकल्पोदयस्तत् ॥ ४५ ॥
transliteration:
pṛṣṭha-śūnyaṃ mūla-śūnyaṃ hṛc-śūnyaṃ bhāvayed drutam |
yugapannirvikalpatvān nirvikalpodayas tataḥ || 45 ||
translation: One should swiftly contemplate the void of the back, the void of the root, and the void of the heart; through simultaneous freedom from conceptualization, there arises the emergence of nonconceptual awareness.
intent_summary: Accelerate into three inner voids until conceptual thought drops away and nonconceptual awareness appears.
beginner_explanation: This verse expands the previous practice by including the heart. Imagine openness behind you, at the base, and in the chest all at once. When you do this without making it into a mental picture contest, the mind can settle into clear, quiet presence.
scholar_explanation: Adding hṛc-śūnya, the heart-space, the verse links multiple internal loci into a single contemplative field. The phrase yugapat nirvikalpatva shows that simultaneity, not sequential effort, triggers nirvikalpa-udaya, the arising of nonconceptuality. This is an important VBT pattern: distributed attention collapses the ordinary center of selfhood.

speaker: Unknown
title: Momentary Emptiness in the Body
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
तनूदेशे शून्यतैि क्षणमािं विभाियेत् ।
वनविधकल्पं वनविधकल्पो वनविधकल्पस्वरूपभाक् ॥ ४६ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava-tantram |
tanūdeśe śūnyatāiva kṣaṇamātraṃ vibhāvayet |
nirvikalpaṃ nirvikalpo nirvikalpa-svarūpa-bhāk || 46 ||
translation: In the region of the body one should contemplate only emptiness for just a moment. [Then] one becomes free of conceptualization, a possessor of the nature of nonconceptuality.
intent_summary: Glimpse emptiness directly in the body long enough for the mind to reveal its own nonconceptual nature.
beginner_explanation: You do not need a long meditation here; just briefly notice empty space within the body. Even a very short pause can interrupt mental chatter. If you repeat it gently, you may notice that awareness itself is naturally clear and quiet.
scholar_explanation: This verse is a terse instruction in kṣaṇamātra-vibhāvanā: a momentary contemplation of śūnyatā in tanūdeśa, the bodily field. The text emphasizes that even a brief encounter with void can disclose nirvikalpa-svarūpa, the inherent form of non-discursive awareness. It is a classic example of the VBT’s confidence in instantaneous recognition rather than prolonged constructivist practice.

speaker: Unknown
title: Body Filled with Space
sanskrit:
सिं देहगतं द्रव्यं वियद्व्याप्तं मृगेक्षणे ।
विभाियेत्ततस्तस्य भािना सा वस्थरा भिेत् ॥ ४७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava-tantram |
sarvaṃ dehagataṃ dravyaṃ viyad-vyāptaṃ mṛgekṣaṇe |
vibhāvayet tataḥ tasya bhāvanā sā sthirā bhavet || 47 ||
translation: O deer-eyed one, one should contemplate that all substances within the body are pervaded by space; then that contemplation becomes steady.
intent_summary: See the body as permeated by open space until this perception becomes stable.
beginner_explanation: Instead of feeling the body as solid and cramped, imagine that it is full of openness and room. You are not trying to deny the body, but to sense it as spacious from within. If you keep returning to this, the feeling can become steady and natural.
scholar_explanation: The verse asks the practitioner to vibhāvayet viyat-vyāptam, envisioning all dehagata dravya as pervaded by space. The address mṛgekṣaṇe softens the instruction with devotional intimacy, while the practice itself erodes substantivist bodily perception. Steady bhāvanā here prepares the cognition of the body as non-solid, compatible with śaiva teachings on the subtle body as luminous openness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Void Within the Body
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
देहान्तरे त्ववविभागम् वभवत्तभूतम् विवचन्तयेत् ।
न वकंवचदन्तरे तस्य ध्यायन्नध्येयभाग्भवेत् ॥ ४८ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava-tantram |
dehāntare tv avibhāgaṃ bhāvita-bhūtam vicintayet |
na kiṃcid antare tasya dhyāyann adhyeya-bhāg bhavet || 48 ||
translation: One should contemplate the undivided nature within the body as a fully established reality. Meditating that there is nothing at all inside it, one becomes a participant in the unmeditated state.
intent_summary: Contemplate the body's inner absence so thoroughly that meditation itself drops into a state beyond deliberate meditation.
beginner_explanation: Look inside and notice that the body’s interior is not a fixed thing; it is open and undivided. When you rest in that sense, there may be no object left to meditate on. Then meditation becomes more like simply being aware than doing a technique.
scholar_explanation: The verse centers dehāntara, the body’s interior, as avibhāga, undividedness, and then radicalizes the insight: na kiṃcit antare, nothing is found within. The result is adhyeya-bhāg, participation in the unmeditated, suggesting a threshold where formal dhyāna collapses into spontaneous awareness. This is consonant with nondual Śaiva pedagogy that uses objectless contemplation to reveal the already-present absolute.

speaker: Unknown
title: Heart Space Between the Palms
sanskrit:
हृद्याकाशे वनलीनाक्ष् पिसम्पुटमध्यग् ।
अनन्यचेता् सुभगे परं सौभावयमाप्नुयात् ॥ ४९ ॥
transliteration:
hṛdyākāśe nilīnākṣaḥ prasampuṭa-madhyagaḥ |
ananyacetāḥ subhage paraṃ saubhāgyam āpnuyāt || 49 ||
translation: With the eyes absorbed in the space of the heart, and centered in the middle of the joined palms, one whose mind is undistracted, O beautiful one, attains supreme blessedness.
intent_summary: Focus the senses into the heart-space and the center of the joined hands to enter undistracted blessedness.
beginner_explanation: Bring your attention to the chest and the space there, while also feeling the center created by placing the palms together. Let your eyes and mind rest there without wandering. This simple centeredness can feel peaceful, intimate, and deeply सुख/fortunate.
scholar_explanation: The verse fuses hṛd-ākāśa with prasampuṭa-madhya, the center of the joined palms, creating a ritualized axis of inward concentration. Nilīnākṣa suggests the eyes have sunk inward, so perception withdraws into the heart-space, yielding paraṃ saubhāgyam, supreme auspiciousness or radiance. This practice is both somatic and devotional, joining mudrā, gaze, and attention.

speaker: Unknown
title: Dissolution at the Twelvefold End
sanskrit:
सिधत् स्वशरीरस्य द्वादशान्ते मनोलयात् ।
दृढिुद्धेदृधढीभूतं तत्त्वलक्ष्यं प्रितधते ॥ ५० ॥
transliteration:
siddhe svadehasya dvādaśānte manolayāt |
dṛḍha-śuddher dṛḍhībhūtaṃ tattva-lakṣyaṃ prapadyate || 50 ||
translation: When the mind dissolves at the twelve-ended point of one's own body, the firmly purified seeker attains the stabilized aim of reality.
intent_summary: Let mind sink at the body’s twelvefold boundary until purified attention rests in the truth of reality.
beginner_explanation: There is a subtle practice of sensing the edges or endpoints of the body and letting the mind become quiet there. As attention settles at that boundary, thoughts can dissolve. What remains is a firmer sense of what is real, beyond mental noise.
scholar_explanation: Dvādaśānta is a key Śaiva/Tantric locus, often the transcendent endpoint of prāṇa or awareness beyond the body’s limits. Through manolaya at this point, dṛḍha-śuddhi matures into dṛḍhībhūta tattva-lakṣya, a stable fixation on reality. The verse marks a transition from spatial contemplations to a more explicitly absorptive dissolution practice.

speaker: Unknown
title: Gaze Beyond the Twelve-Finger Space
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
यथा तथा यि ति द्वादशान्ते मन् वक्षपेत् ॥
प्रवतक्षणम् क्षीणिृत्तेिैलक्षण्यं वदनैभधिेत् ॥ ५१ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
yathā tathā yi ti dvādaśānte man vakṣapet ||
pravatakṣaṇam kṣīṇiṛttueilakṣaṇyaṃ vadanaibhadhiet || 51 ||
translation: In whatever way the mind is thrown into the twelve-finger space, at the instant when mental modifications have weakened, one should behold the distinctionless nature in the face (or opening).
intent_summary: Use the subtle gap at the end of an out-breath or in-breath to notice the mind’s fading and rest in the undivided awareness that appears there.
beginner_explanation: This verse points you to a small pause or open space in breathing or attention, called the twelve-finger space. When the mind quiets there, you are asked to notice a clear, open awareness instead of your usual thoughts. It is like catching the silence between waves.
scholar_explanation: The key is dvādaśānta, the subtle point twelve finger-widths beyond or within the body where prāṇa resolves. As vṛtti weakens (kṣīṇa-vṛtti), one recognizes the viśeṣa-abhāva or 'distinctionless' condition, which the text links with the mukha/appearance of Bhairava-consciousness. This is a classic liminal-breath dhāraṇā in which prāṇa and manas subside together.

speaker: Unknown
title: Contemplate the Burnt City of Time
sanskrit:
कालाविना कालपदादुवत्थतेन स्वकं पुरम् ।
प्लुष्टं विवचन्तयेदन्ते शान्ताभासस्तदा भिेत् ॥ ५२ ॥
transliteration:
kālāvinā kālapadād uvatthena svakaṃ puram |
pluṣṭaṃ vivacintayed ante śāntābhāsas tadā bhiet || 52 ||
translation: Born from the step of time beyond time, one should contemplate one’s own city as burned up; then, at the end, there arises an appearance of peace.
intent_summary: Imagine the entire personal world as consumed and resolved, until a peaceful, quiet radiance arises in its place.
beginner_explanation: This meditation asks you to picture your whole inner and outer world as if it had been burned away. Instead of fear, you stay with the image until what remains is a peaceful feeling or clear stillness. It is a way of letting go of everything temporary.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses a powerful apocalyptic image: svakaṃ puram, the embodied/psychic 'city,' is to be seen as pluṣṭam, burned, by the force of kāla and beyond-kāla. The result is śāntābhāsa, the semblance or radiance of peace, suggesting that when temporal identity is imaginatively dissolved, the mind falls into a tranquil reflection of the Self. This belongs to the visualization-dissolution interface typical of VBT.

speaker: Unknown
title: See the World as Twofold and Unequal
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
एवं एव जगत्सं द्विधं ध्यात्वा विकल्पतः ।
अनन्यचेतस् पुम्स् पुम्भाव् परमो भवेत् ॥ ५३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
evaṃ eva jagat saṃ dvidhaṃ dhyātvā vikalpataḥ |
ananyacetas pums pum bhāvaḥ paramo bhavet || 53 ||
translation: Thus, contemplating the world as divided in two through thought-construction, a person whose mind is without otherness becomes supreme.
intent_summary: Recognize that division is a mental construction, and let attention become non-dual and free of an 'other.'
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the world seems split into many opposites because of thinking. If you see that this split is just a mental habit, your mind can become simple and whole. Then you taste a more elevated state that is beyond inner conflict.
scholar_explanation: Here vikalpa is explicitly named as the basis of jagat-bheda, the apparent dualization of experience. The remedy is ananyacetas, a mind without secondness or alienation, leading to pum-bhāvaḥ paramo—an exalted state of personhood or pure subjectivity unmarked by objectification. The teaching aligns with Śaiva nonduality: difference is not denied empirically but recognized as a construction within consciousness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Merge Subtle Tattvas in the Body or World
sanskrit:
स्वदेहे जगतो वापि सूक्ष्मसूक्ष्मतराणि च ।
तत्त्वानि यानि विलयं ध्यात्वान्ते व्यज्यते परा ॥ ५४ ॥
transliteration:
svadehe jagato vāpi sūkṣmasūkṣmatarāṇi ca |
tattvāni yāni vilayaṃ dhyātvānte vyajyate parā || 54 ||
translation: In one’s own body or in the world, whatever extremely subtle principles there are, by meditating on their dissolution, the supreme reality is then revealed.
intent_summary: Trace even the subtlest components of experience back into dissolution until the highest reality shines forth.
beginner_explanation: This practice invites you to look at the tiniest levels of your body or the world and imagine them dissolving. Instead of trying to hold onto things, you let them soften and disappear into source. In that openness, something deeper becomes visible.
scholar_explanation: The verse extends dhyāna to sūkṣma and sūkṣmatarā tattvas, whether located in deha or jagat, and instructs vilaya-dhyāna, meditation on dissolution. The culmination is parā, the supreme Śakti or transcendent reality that manifests when analytic structures of manifestation are mentally reabsorbed. It resonates with tattva-laya doctrines across Kashmir Śaivism.

speaker: Unknown
title: Enter the Heart Through the Twelvefold Field
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
पीनां च दुिधलां शविं ध्यात्वा द्वादशगोचरे ।
प्रविश्य हृदये ध्यायन्मुि् स्वातन्त्र्यमाप्नुयात् ॥ ५५ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
pīnāṃ ca duidhalāṃ śaviṃ dhyātvā dvādaśagochare |
praviśya hṛdaye dhyāyan muḍ svātantryam āpnuyāt || 55 ||
translation: Meditating on the gross and subtle power as having two parts within the field of the twelve, then entering into the heart and meditating, one attains freedom.
intent_summary: Use awareness of body and subtle energy in the twelvefold field to draw attention into the heart and realize inner freedom.
beginner_explanation: This verse suggests focusing on your body and its subtle energy, not as separate, but as something you can trace inward. By bringing attention into the heart, you move from outer feeling to a deeper inner center. The result is freedom, not because anything was forced, but because attention returned home.
scholar_explanation: The reading is difficult, but the practice appears to involve dhyāna on śakti as dual or bipartite within the dvādaśa-gochara, then praveśa into hṛdaya. Hṛdaya here is the Śaiva center of consciousness, not merely the physical organ, and the result is svātantrya, the hallmark of Bhairava’s own freedom. The verse links bodily-subtle contemplation with the heart-doctrine central to Trika.

speaker: Unknown
title: Trace the World Through the Cosmic Channels
sanskrit:
भुिनार्ध्वावदरूपेण वचन्तयेत्क्रमशोऽवखलम् ।
स्थूलसूक्ष्मपरवस्थत्या यािदन्ते मनोलय् ॥ ५६ ॥
transliteration:
bhuvanārdhvāvadarūpeṇa vicintayet kramaśo'khilam |
sthūlasūkṣmaparāvasthatyā yāvad ante manolayaḥ || 56 ||
translation: One should contemplate the entire universe successively as the form of the cosmic channels, until, through the states gross, subtle, and supreme, there is finally the dissolution of mind.
intent_summary: Contemplate reality as moving through layered levels of manifestation until thought dissolves completely.
beginner_explanation: Here you gradually look at the whole universe as if it were arranged in a sacred pattern or pathway. You then move through bigger and smaller levels of experience, from obvious to subtle to deepest. If you stay with that process, the mind eventually quiets down on its own.
scholar_explanation: Bhuvana and ūrdhva/adhvan terminology suggest an ordered contemplative mapping of the cosmos onto the practitioner’s inner path. The gradual movement through sthūla, sūkṣma, and parā avasthā culminates in manolaya, a dissolution of mental activity rather than mere conceptual understanding. This is a classic graded visualization that ends in absorption.

speaker: Unknown
title: Contemplate Shiva as the Inner Principle of All Paths
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
अस्य सिधस्य विश्वस्य पयधन्तेषु समन्तत् ।
अर्ध्वप्रवक्रयया तत्त्वं शैिं ध्यत्वा महोदय् ॥ ५७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
asya siddhasya viśvasya paryanteṣu samantataḥ |
ūrdhvaprakriyayā tattvaṃ śaivaṃ dhyātvā mahodayam || 57 ||
translation: At the limits of this accomplished universe, everywhere, by the upward method one should meditate on the Śaiva principle; thus there is great awakening.
intent_summary: At the boundaries of experience, rise through the inner path and recognize Shiva-consciousness everywhere.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that at the edges of the world or of your experience, you can practice an upward turning of attention. When you do this, you are not just thinking about Shiva; you are recognizing a deeper principle that is already present. That recognition brings a big inner opening or awakening.
scholar_explanation: The verse situates practice at the paryanta, the edges or endpoints of the siddha viśva, and uses ūrdhva-prakriyā, the upward movement central to ascent-oriented Śaiva methods. By meditating on tattvaṃ śaivam, one realizes mahodaya, the great rising or expansion of consciousness. The emphasis is on immanent transcendence: the same Śiva-principle permeates the totality and is accessed through upwardly directed awareness.

speaker: Unknown
title: See the Universe as Empty
sanskrit:
विश्वमेतन्महादेवि शून्यभूतं विवचन्तयेत् ।
तिैि च मनो लीनं ततस्तल्लयभाजनम् ॥ ५८ ॥
transliteration:
viśvam etan mahādevi śūnyabhūtaṃ vivicintayet |
tatraiva ca mano līnaṃ tatas tallayabhājanam || 58 ||
translation: O Great Goddess, one should contemplate this universe as become empty; then the mind becomes absorbed there, and thereby it becomes a vessel of that dissolution.
intent_summary: Perceive the universe as empty space so the mind can sink into that emptiness and become fit for dissolution.
beginner_explanation: This meditation asks you to see everything as empty, not dead, but open and ungraspable. When you rest in that openness, your mind naturally settles into it. In time, you become more and more aligned with that quiet spaciousness.
scholar_explanation: Śūnyabhūtaṃ viśvam is not nihilism but a contemplative deconstruction of fixed appearance into openness. The mind, once placed there, becomes līna and then a bhājana, a 'receptacle' for laya, indicating a refined receptivity to absorption. The verse exemplifies the Vajrayāna-like Śaiva use of śūnya as a doorway to consciousness rather than an endpoint of negation.

speaker: Unknown
title: Drop the Gaze into the Container Wall
sanskrit:
घटावदभाजने दृवष्टं वभवत्तस्त्यक्त्वा विवनवक्षपेत् ।
तल्लयं तत्क्षणाद्गत्वा तल्लयात्तन्मयो भिेत् ॥ ५९ ॥
transliteration:
ghaṭāvadbhājane dṛṣṭiṃ vibhavattasy tyaktvā vinikṣipet |
tallayaṃ tatkṣaṇād gatvā tallayāt tanmayo bhavet || 59 ||
translation: Abandon the gaze, which is like the wall in a pot-like vessel, and cast it in; instantly going into that dissolution, from that dissolution one becomes identified with That.
intent_summary: Release the normal way of seeing and sink awareness inward until it merges with the deeper reality it contacts.
beginner_explanation: Think of your usual attention as the hard wall of a container. This verse asks you to let that boundary go and let awareness fall inward, beyond the usual edge. When that happens, you no longer feel separate from what you are experiencing.
scholar_explanation: The imagery is of dṛṣṭi as a boundary-wall within the ghaṭa-like body or perceptual container. By tyaktvā and vinikṣipet, sight is intentionally dropped into the interior, producing tatkṣaṇa laya and then tanmaya, identity with That. This is a concise instruction in perceptual self-transcendence through immediate inward collapse of the subject-object frame.

speaker: Unknown
title: Fix the Gaze in a Crack or Gap
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
वनिृधक्षवगवरवभत्त्यावददेशे दृवष्टं विवनवक्षपेत् ।
विलीने मानसे भािे िृत्तिक्षीण् प्रजायते ॥ ६० ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
niruddhāgvaravibhittyādideśe dṛṣṭiṃ vinikṣipet |
vilīne mānase bhāve vṛttikṣīṇaḥ prajāyate || 60 ||
translation: One should cast the gaze into a place such as a crevice or gap in a closed wall. When the mental state has dissolved, the stream of thought becomes exhausted.
intent_summary: Use a literal visual gap or crack as a support for attention until the mind dissolves and thought subsides.
beginner_explanation: This verse uses a simple trick: look at a small crack, gap, or opening in front of you. Keep your attention there until your mind becomes still and thought loses its momentum. The outer gap helps reveal the inner gap.
scholar_explanation: The instruction employs external śūnya-like breaks in a closed surface as visual supports for internalization of awareness. Once the mānasa-bhāva is vilīna, vṛtti-kṣaya follows naturally, revealing awareness beyond discursive motion. The verse links sensory fixation on a gap with the cessation of mental proliferation, echoing other sandhi-based practices in the VBT.

speaker: Unknown
title: Center Between Dualities
sanskrit:
उभयोभाधियोज्ञाधने ध्यात्वा मध्यं समाश्रयेत् ।
युगपच्च द्वयं त्यक्त्वा मध्ये तत्त्वं प्रकाशते ॥ ६१ ॥
transliteration:
ubhayor bhādayor jñādhane dhyātvā madhyaṃ samāśrayet |
yugapat ca dvayaṃ tyaktvā madhye tattvaṃ prakāśate || 61 ||
translation: Having meditated on the two sides and knowing them, one should take refuge in the middle. When both dualities are abandoned at once, the Reality shines in the middle.
intent_summary: To direct attention to the living center that appears when both sides of a duality are released.
beginner_explanation: This verse says not to get stuck on either side of a pair of opposites. Instead, notice the point in between, like the still place between two swinging motions. When you let both sides go together, something clear and quiet becomes visible there.
scholar_explanation: The instruction is a classic madhya-upāya: by examining both poles of experience and then relinquishing them simultaneously, consciousness is established in the madhya where tattva manifests. This is not a spatial midpoint only, but the nondual center of awareness beyond alternate conceptualizing. It resonates with VBT passages on the junctions of breath and the gaps between thoughts.

speaker: Unknown
title: Rest in the Gap After Dropping Mental States
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
भावे त्यक्ते निरुद्धा चित्तं नैव भावान्तरं व्रजेत् ।
तदा तन्मध्यभावेन विकसत्यतिभावना ॥ ६२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tant्रम |
bhāve tyakte niruddhaṃ cittaṃ naiva bhāvāntaraṃ vrajet |
tadā tanmadhyabhāvena vikasaty atibhāvanā || 62 ||
translation: When an object or state is let go and the mind is restrained, and it does not move to another state, then by that middle condition supreme contemplation unfolds.
intent_summary: To let one mental content end without immediately replacing it, allowing deeper awareness to open.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to the pause after a thought or feeling fades, before the next one takes over. If you stay there instead of rushing to the next thing, the mind opens like a flower. That open pause is the practice.
scholar_explanation: Here bhāva is released and citta is nirodhita, but the key is that it does not immediately shift into another bhāvāntara. The resulting tanmadhyabhāva is a fertile interval in which atibhāvanā—intense or supreme contemplative flowering—appears. The verse aligns with the Tantric use of interruption, not suppression, as a doorway to recognition.

speaker: Unknown
title: Perceive the Body as Consciousness
sanskrit:
सिं देहं चिन्मयं हि जगद्वा परिभावयेत् ।
युगपन्निविधकल्पेन मनसा परमोदयः ॥ ६३ ॥
transliteration:
svaṃ dehaṃ cinmayaṃ hi jagad vā paribhāvayet |
yugapan nividha-kalpena manasā paramodayaḥ || 63 ||
translation: One should contemplate one’s own body as made of consciousness, or the world likewise. With the mind holding both views at once, the supreme arising occurs.
intent_summary: To train perception so that body and world are seen as expressions of consciousness, not separate from it.
beginner_explanation: This verse invites you to look at your body and the world as if they were made of the same clear awareness. You can hold both ideas together: “this body is consciousness” and “this world is consciousness.” When that happens, a deeper sense of being can appear.
scholar_explanation: The practice is cidekātmatā-bhāvanā: deha and jagat are re-envisioned as cinmaya, consisting of consciousness. The phrase yugapat indicates simultaneous apprehension without exclusion, which destabilizes habitual objectification. Paramodaya is the “supreme emergence” of nondual insight, a recognition central to Trika epistemology.

speaker: Unknown
title: Arising Through the Two Winds
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
िायुद्वयस्य सम्घट्टाद् अन्तर् िा िवहरन्तत् ।
योगी समत्वविज्ञानसमुद्गमनभाजनम् ॥ ६४ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tant्रम |
prāṇāpānadvayasya saṅghaṭṭād antar vā viharantat |
yogī samatvavijñāna-samudgamanabhājanam || 64 ||
translation: By the collision of the two breaths, prāṇa and apāna, or by their movement inward, the yogī becomes a vessel for the arising of equal awareness.
intent_summary: To use the meeting or balancing of breath currents as a doorway to equal, spacious awareness.
