beginner_explanation: Your breathing has two sides: one that rises and one that descends. When they meet or balance, there can be a natural stillness. This verse says to use that moment to rest in balanced awareness.
scholar_explanation: The verse points to prāṇa-apāna-saṅghaṭṭa, the internal meeting of opposing vital currents, as a trigger for samatva-vijñāna. The OCR is imperfect, but the dhāraṇā clearly belongs to breath-polarity practices common in the VBT. The yogin becomes a bhājana, a “vessel,” for equalized consciousness when the dual movement is resolved.

speaker: Unknown
title: See the World as the Blissful Body of Self
sanskrit:
सिं जगत्स्वदेहं िा स्वानन्दभवरतं स्मरेत् ।
युगपत्स्वामृतेनैि परानन्दमयो भिेत् ॥ ६५ ॥
transliteration:
svaṃ jagat sva-dehaṃ vā svānandabhavarataṃ smaret |
yugapat svāmṛtenaiva parānandamayo bhavet || 65 ||
translation: One should remember the world, or one’s own body, as abiding in one’s own bliss. By one’s own nectar at once, one becomes filled with supreme bliss.
intent_summary: To reframe body and world as immersed in one’s own innate bliss, leading to expanded joy.
beginner_explanation: This verse suggests that the world and your body can be remembered as resting in deep happiness, not as separate or threatening. If you taste that inner sweetness directly, it can overflow into everything you experience. The result is a larger, more complete joy.
scholar_explanation: The practice is ananda-bhāvanā: jagat and deha are recollected as svānandabhavarata, “delighting in one’s own blissful being.” Through svāmṛta—one’s own nectar or immortality—the practitioner becomes parānandamaya, filled with supreme bliss. This is not mere emotion but a nondual revaluation of phenomenal appearance through innate ānanda.

speaker: Unknown
title: Sudden Great Bliss Through Skillful Means
sanskrit:
कुहनेन प्रयोगेण सद्य एि मृगेक्षणे ।
समुदेवत महानन्दो येन तत्त्वम् प्रकाशते ॥ ६६ ॥
transliteration:
kuhanena prayogeṇa sadya eva mṛgekṣaṇe |
samudbhūtaṃ mahānando yena tattvam prakāśate || 66 ||
translation: O lotus-eyed one, by an artful method, great bliss arises at once, by which the Truth becomes manifest.
intent_summary: To evoke immediate bliss through an effective technique, allowing truth to reveal itself.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that a well-chosen method can bring a sudden wave of joy. That joy is not the goal by itself; it helps reveal what is most real. Think of it as a shortcut that opens the door quickly.
scholar_explanation: Kuhana here suggests a subtle or ingenious upāya rather than deception in the ordinary sense. Mahānanda arises suddenly and serves as a revelatory condition for tattva-prakāśa, the shining forth of reality. The vocative mṛgekṣaṇe shows the embodied, devotional setting of Tantric instruction.

speaker: Unknown
title: Rising the Breath Through the Inner Stream
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सिधस्रोतोवनिन्धेन प्राणशक्त्योर्ध्वधया शनैः ।
वपपीलस्पशधिेलायां प्रथते परमं सुखम् ॥ ६७ ॥
transliteration:
sahasrasrotoviniṣṭhena prāṇaśaktyordhvadhā śanaiḥ |
pipīlikā-sparśavelāyāṃ prathate paramaṃ sukham || 67 ||
translation: When the prāṇa-shakti slowly moves upward through the channel that is blocked by a thousand streams, then at the time of the ant’s touch, supreme delight becomes manifest.
intent_summary: To guide subtle life-energy upward into a fine, barely perceptible sensation where deep joy can arise.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a very delicate inner feeling, like the light touch of an ant. By gently lifting the breath-energy upward, a subtle joy can appear. The practice is to be soft and attentive rather than forceful.
scholar_explanation: The text describes prāṇaśakti’s ūrdhvadhā, its upward course, through the obstructed sahasrasrota pathway. Pipīlikā-sparśa indicates a nearly imperceptible tactile threshold, a classical marker for subtle somatic awareness. The emergence of paramaṃ sukham shows how fine prāṇic refinement can open into transcendent delight.

speaker: Unknown
title: Cast the Mind Into the Fire of Bliss
sanskrit:
िह्नेविधषस्य मध्ये तु वचत्तं सुखमयं वक्षपेत् ।
केिलं िायुपूणं िा स्मरानन्देन युज्यते ॥ ६८ ॥
transliteration:
vahneḥ viṣayasya madhye tu cittaṃ sukhamayaṃ kṣipet |
kevalaṃ vāyupūrṇaṃ vā smarānandena yujyate || 68 ||
translation: In the midst of the fire of sense-objects, one should cast the mind as made of bliss. Or, filled only with breath, one is joined with the bliss of remembrance.
intent_summary: To transform sensory heat or inner fullness into blissful remembrance rather than distraction.
beginner_explanation: When strong sensations or desires feel like a fire, don’t fight them. Place the mind there as if it were made of happiness, and the fire can become fuel for peace. Even simply feeling full and alive with breath can open into remembrance and joy.
scholar_explanation: The verse counsels converting viṣaya-agnitva into sukhamaya-citta, thereby transmuting sensuous intensity rather than avoiding it. Alternatively, kevala-vāyu-pūrṇatā creates an internally saturated field in which smara-ananda—bliss of recollection—arises. This is a Tantric sacralization of experience rather than a withdrawal from it.

speaker: Unknown
title: Bliss in Union of Power and Beloved
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
शविसंगमसंक्षुब्धशक्त्यािेशािसावनकम् ।
यत्सुखम् ब्रह्मतत्त्वस्य तत्सुखम् स्वाक्यमुच्यते ॥ ६९ ॥
transliteration:
śakti-saṅgama-saṃkṣubdha-śaktyāveśāvasānikaḥ |
yat sukhaṃ brahmatattvasya tat sukhaṃ svākhyam ucyate || 69 ||
translation: The bliss that comes at the conclusion of the absorption of power, stirred by the union of Śakti, is declared to be the bliss of Brahma-tattva.
intent_summary: To recognize intense sacred bliss as a manifestation of ultimate reality, not merely personal pleasure.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that profound joy arising in union or powerful inner energy is not ordinary excitement. It is connected with something absolute and sacred. If you recognize that, the feeling becomes a doorway to the deepest truth.
scholar_explanation: Śakti-saṅgama and śaktyāveśa indicate the ritualized or experiential conjunction of power, culminating in a bliss identified with brahmatattva. The verse maps erotic-devotional intensity onto metaphysical realization, a hallmark of Kaula and Trika hermeneutics. Svākhyam here signals a self-named, self-evident bliss that is intrinsic to the Absolute.

speaker: Unknown
title: Remember Bliss in Erotic Union
sanskrit:
लेहनामन्थनाकोटै् स्त्रीसुखस्य भरात्स्मृते् ।
शक्त्यभािेऽवप देिेवश भिेदानन्दसम्प्लि् ॥ ७० ॥
transliteration:
lehanā-manthana-koṭaiḥ strī-sukhasya bharāt smṛteḥ |
śaktyabhāve'pi deveśi bhaved ānanda-samplavaḥ || 70 ||
translation: By the overflowing remembrance of the bliss of woman through licking, churning, and the like, O Lord of the gods, even in the absence of actual power there can arise a flood of bliss.
intent_summary: To use remembrance and subtle bodily memory of sexual bliss as a means for awakening inner bliss.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to the way memory can bring back a powerful feeling, even when the situation itself is absent. By remembering intense pleasure with full attention, a wave of joy can arise again. The point is not the act itself, but the awareness it awakens.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes erotic memory—strī-sukha-smṛti—as a contemplative support, even śaktyabhāve, when the external condition is absent. In Kaula vocabulary, the senses and memory become means for ānanda-samplava, an inundation of bliss that is ultimately spiritualized. The address to deveśi frames the teaching within the goddess-centered tantric discourse.

speaker: Unknown
title: Bliss-Absorption into Its Source
sanskrit:
आनन्दे महवत प्राप्ते दृष्टे िा िान्धिे वचरात् ।
आनन्दमुद्गतम् ध्यात्वा तल्लयस्तन्मना भिेत् ॥ ७१ ॥
transliteration:
ānande mahati prāpte dṛṣṭe vā bandhave cirāt |
ānandam udbhūtaṃ dhyātvā tal-layas tan-manā bhavet || 71 ||
translation: When great bliss has arisen, whether from seeing a loved one after a long time or from some other cause, one should meditate on that bliss as rising up; then, absorbed in it, the mind becomes one with it.
intent_summary: Use an intense experience of joy as a doorway into meditative absorption by staying with the bliss until mind merges into it.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that when you feel a strong wave of happiness, don’t immediately run after the story behind it. Instead, notice the feeling itself and rest in it. If you stay with the pure feeling, your mind can dissolve into that joy.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses ānanda as an ālambana for laya: the practitioner contemplates the arising of bliss (udbhūtaṃ dhyātvā) and allows tan-laya, absorption into that very state. This is a classic Tantric use of affective intensity as a support for nondual recognition, where emotional exhilaration is not rejected but refined into consciousness. Related dhāraṇās often treat rasa, pleasure, and surprise as portals to Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Bliss from Union and Delight
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
जववधपानकृतोल्लासरसानन्दविजृम्भणात् ।
भाियेद्भवरतािस्थां महानन्दस्ततो भिेत् ॥ ७२ ॥
transliteration:
japavidhyāna-pāna-kṛtollāsa-rasa-ānanda-vijṛmbhaṇāt |
bhāvayed bhairavīṃ āvasthāṃ mahānandas tato bhavet || 72 ||
translation: From the delight produced by mantra, meditation, and drinking, and from the expansion of the taste of bliss, one should contemplate the Bhairavī state; then great bliss arises.
intent_summary: Transform intensified pleasure or exhilaration into contemplation of the divine feminine state, allowing that bliss to open into greater spiritual joy.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to moments when practice, ritual, or even a sensory experience makes you feel lifted up. Instead of clinging to the enjoyment, turn attention toward the deeper sacred feeling behind it. By doing so, the pleasure becomes a gateway to a much larger joy.
scholar_explanation: The text links japa, dhyāna, and pāna to an expanded rasa of ānanda, then directs the yogin to bhairavīṃ āvasthām, the empowered conscious state. Whether pāna is literal or symbolic, the point is transmutation of intensified rasa into a contemplative recognition of Śakti as blissful consciousness. The resultant mahānanda is not mere emotion but an emergence of the nondual vivification of awareness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Taste the Equal Joy of All Experience
sanskrit:
वगतावदविषयास्वादासमसौख्यैकतात्मन् ।
योवगनस्तन्मयत्वेन मनोरूढेस् तदात्मता ॥ ७३ ॥
transliteration:
gīta-ādi-viṣaya-āsvāda-asama-saukhya-eka-tātman |
yoginas tanmayatvena mano-rūḍheṣ tad-ātmatā || 73 ||
translation: For the yogin whose nature has become one-pointed through identification with that which is tasted in music and other sense-objects, when the mind is established there, that very identity is his own nature.
intent_summary: Use aesthetic or sensory enjoyment to enter single-pointed identification and recognize the self in the experience itself.
beginner_explanation: When music, art, or any sense experience becomes deeply absorbing, this verse says to stay with that total involvement. If the mind settles fully into the experience, the feeling of “me” and the feeling of what is experienced can begin to merge. That merger reveals a deeper unity underneath both.
scholar_explanation: Here viṣaya-āsvāda is not treated as bondage but as a yogic doorway when integrated into eka-tātman and tanmayatva. The verse proposes that manoruḍhi—mind stabilized in the tasted object—leads to tad-ātmatā, identity with the object as a vehicle for self-recognition. This is a subtle nondual move: sensory delight is not denied, but used to dissolve the rigid subject-object split.

speaker: Unknown
title: Any Surge of Contentment
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
यि यि मनस्तुवष्टमधनस्तिैि धारयेत् ।
ति ति परानन्दस्वारूपं सम्प्रितधते ॥ ७४ ॥
transliteration:
yatra yatra manaḥ tuṣṭi-mātraṃ tatr eva dhārayet |
tatra tatra parānanda-svarūpaṃ sampravartate || 74 ||
translation: Wherever and whenever there is only a simple satisfaction of the mind, there one should hold it there; there and then the nature of supreme bliss manifests.
intent_summary: Notice any natural contentment, however small, and hold attention there until it unfolds into higher bliss.
beginner_explanation: This verse teaches that even a small feeling of “this is enough” can be used in meditation. When the mind feels quietly satisfied, don’t rush past it. Stay with that feeling, and it can open into a deeper sense of peace and joy.
scholar_explanation: Tuṣṭi here functions as a subtle śānti-like gateway into parānanda-svarūpa, the essential nature of supreme bliss. The yogin does not manufacture an altered state; rather, he stabilizes attention wherever the mind is naturally content, allowing the latent fullness of consciousness to reveal itself. The dhāraṇā is therefore minimalist and phenomenological, using ordinary satisfaction as a trigger for recognition.

speaker: Unknown
title: Meditation in the Pre-Sleep Gap
sanskrit:
अनागतायां वनद्रायां प्रणष्टे िाह्यगोचरे ।
सािस्था मनसा गम्या परा देिी प्रकाशते ॥ ७५ ॥
transliteration:
anāgatāyāṃ nidrāyāṃ praṇaṣṭe bāhya-gochare |
sāvasthā manasā gamyā parā devī prakāśate || 75 ||
translation: When sleep has not yet arrived and the outer field has disappeared, that state is to be reached by the mind; there the supreme Goddess shines forth.
intent_summary: Enter the liminal space just before sleep, when outer perception fades, and use awareness to recognize the luminous देवी-consciousness there.
beginner_explanation: Right before you fall asleep, the world starts to fade but you are still somewhat aware. This verse says to notice that in-between state instead of losing it. If you remain present there, a deeper presence can become clear.
scholar_explanation: The focus is the twilight condition of anāgatā nidrā, when external objects have fallen away (praṇaṣṭe bāhya-gocare) yet awareness has not collapsed into ordinary sleep. This liminal interval is prized in Tantra because it resembles a natural withdrawal of vṛttis, allowing parā devī prakāśate—the supreme luminous Power—to manifest. It aligns with other VBT methods using thresholds between waking and sleep as direct portals to turīya.

speaker: Unknown
title: Gaze into the Luminous Sky
sanskrit:
तेजसा सूयधदीपादेराकाशे शिलीकृते ।
दृवष्टवनधिेश्या तिैि स्वात्मरूपं प्रकाशते ॥ ७६ ॥
transliteration:
tejasā sūrya-dīpāder ākāśe śakalīkṛte |
dṛṣṭir niveśyā tatraiva sva-ātma-rūpaṃ prakāśate || 76 ||
translation: When the sky is made radiant by the light of the sun, a lamp, or the like, one should fix the gaze there; then one's own self-form shines forth.
intent_summary: Use a luminous outer field as a mirror for self-recognition by resting the gaze in bright space until the self appears as light.
beginner_explanation: This verse suggests looking into a bright, open field such as the sky or a radiant light. Instead of staring hard, let your gaze settle gently into the brightness. As attention becomes quiet, you may sense your own inner self as something luminous and spacious.
scholar_explanation: The external tejas of sun or lamp renders ākāśa as a support for dṛṣṭi-niveśa. The point is not optical fascination but the de-centering of ordinary visual grasping, so that sva-ātma-rūpa—the self as luminous awareness—appears. This is a classic śākta visualization/trataka-like dhāraṇā in which outer light reveals inner light.

speaker: Unknown
title: Khechari Gaze into the Fierce Mouth
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
करवङ्कण्या क्रोधनया भैरव्या लेलिहानया ।
खेचयाध दृवष्टकाले च परािावप्त् प्रकाशते ॥ ७७ ॥
transliteration:
karaṅkinyā krodhanayā bhairavyā lelihānayā |
khecaryā dṛṣṭi-kāle ca parā-vāptiḥ prakāśate || 77 ||
translation: By the fierce, wrathful, lapping Bhairavī, and by the gaze of khecarī, supreme attainment shines forth at the time of seeing.
intent_summary: Concentrate the gaze in a charged, upward, and liminal way so that vision itself becomes a doorway to supreme realization.
beginner_explanation: This verse uses vivid, fierce imagery to point to a powerful kind of focused seeing. Khechari means the gaze or attention is lifted beyond ordinary looking. When that happens, the sense of reaching something highest or beyond appears naturally.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes Bhairavī in a krodhana/lelihāna aspect and couples it with khecarī-dṛṣṭi, a gaze that abides in the 'moving in space' mode of awareness. Parā-vāpti here indicates not acquisition but recognition of the highest state through the very act of seeing. The fierce imagery emphasizes that transcendence can emerge through intense, non-ordinary attention rather than calm neutrality alone.

speaker: Unknown
title: Supported Unburdening of the Limbs
sanskrit:
मृद्वासने विजैकेन हस्तपादौ वनराश्रयम् ।
वनधाय तत्प्रसङ्गेन परा पूणाध मवतभधिेत् ॥ ७८ ॥
transliteration:
mṛdv-āsane vijāikeṇa hastapādau nirāśrayam |
nidhāya tat-prasaṅgena parā pūrṇā matir bhavet || 78 ||
translation: Seated on a soft seat, with the hands and feet unsupported, placing them without reliance, through that condition a supreme, पूर्णā mind arises.
intent_summary: Relax the body's support and let the limbs rest without effort so that the mind naturally becomes full and spacious.
beginner_explanation: Sit comfortably and let your hands and feet rest without holding them rigidly. The point is to feel the body becoming less controlled and more open. In that ease, the mind can become calm, full, and settled.
scholar_explanation: This verse uses bodily release, nirāśrayam, as a trigger for parā pūrṇā mati, the fullness of mind that is not fragmented by effort. The physical condition of unsupported limbs reduces muscular striving and thus softens the sense of agency tied to embodiment. In VBT terms, the body is not opposed to realization; rather, embodied ease is a direct support for expanded awareness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Shoulders Raised into Inner Quiet
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
उपविश्यासने सम्यविाहू कृत्वाधधकुवञ्चतौ ।
कक्षव्योवि मन् कुिधन् शममायावत तल्लयात् ॥ ७९ ॥
transliteration:
upaviśyāsane samyag bāhū kṛtvārdhakuñcitau |
kakṣa-vyomaṇi man kurvan śamam āyāti tal-layāt || 79 ||
translation: Sitting properly on the seat, with the arms slightly bent, and making the mind into the space of the armpits, one attains quietude through absorption in that.
intent_summary: Bring attention into a subtle bodily space and let the mind settle there until deep calm and absorption arise.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to notice a small, often ignored part of the body: the space around the armpits and upper torso. By resting attention there, the mind stops scattering so much. That focused inner feeling leads to quiet.
scholar_explanation: Kakṣa-vyomaṇi man kurvan directs awareness to an intermediate bodily void, a localized 'space' within embodiment. This is a refined somatic dhāraṇā: attention is neither on gross posture nor abstract thought, but on a subtle bodily cavity that catalyzes tal-laya and śama. The method shows how interior space within the body can become a support for absorption.

speaker: Unknown
title: Fixation on the Gross Form
sanskrit:
स्थूलरूपस्य भािस्य स्तब्धां दृवष्टं वनपात्य च ।
अवचरेण वनराधारं मन् कृत्वा वशिं व्रजेत् ॥ ८० ॥
transliteration:
sthūla-rūpasya bhāvasya stabdhāṃ dṛṣṭiṃ nipātya ca |
acareṇa nirādhāraṃ man kṛtvā śivaṃ vrajet || 80 ||
translation: Casting the gaze, motionless, upon the gross form of an object, and making the mind supportless through the unmoving [gaze], one goes to Śiva.
intent_summary: Stabilize the gaze on a gross object until the mind becomes still and unsupported, leading into Śiva-consciousness.
beginner_explanation: Choose a visible object and look at it without moving your eyes around. As the gaze becomes steady, the mind also becomes less restless. When that happens, the sense of a separate self can quiet down and a deeper presence can emerge.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses stabdhā dṛṣṭi on sthūla-rūpa to produce nirādhāra manas, a mind without conceptual supports. The 'immobile' gaze suspends normal perceptual scanning and thereby deconstructs the mind's habitual attachment to objects. The result is not blankness but entry into śiva, the nondual ground of awareness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Inner Repetition at the Jaws
sanskrit:
मध्यवजह्वे िावरतास्ये मध्ये वनक्षप्य चेतनाम् ।
होच्चारं मनसा कुिंस्तत् शान्ते प्रलीयते ॥ ८१ ॥
transliteration:
madhyavaj-jihve vārttāsye madhye vinikṣipya cetanām |
hochcāraṃ manasā kuryāt śānte pralīyate || 81 ||
translation: Placing awareness in the middle of the tongue and the palate, one should mentally make the sound of the upward exhalation (hoch-cāra); when it becomes शांत (pacified), one dissolves into it.
intent_summary: Use attention on the tongue-palate center and the subtle upward breath-sound to let the mind subside into stillness.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a small but vivid inner focus: the place where the tongue and palate meet, along with the feeling of the breath or sound moving upward. By gently holding attention there, the mind becomes quieter. When the inner motion settles down, awareness can sink into a calm, spacious stillness.
scholar_explanation: The practice is a tongue-palate locus meditation combined with subtle uccāra/hochcāra, likely an internalized breath-sound or mantra-gesture. By placing cetanā in the madhya of the jivhā-vartta/tālu region, the practitioner enters a liminal point where prāṇa and vāc converge. The result is pralaya into śānta, a classic VBT move from supported concentration into absorptive stillness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Resting in Unsupported Being
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
आसने शयने वस्थत्वा वनराधारं विभाियन् ।
स्वदेहं मनवस वक्षणे क्षणात्क्षीणाशयो भिेत् ॥ ८२ ॥
transliteration:
āsane śayane vā sthitvā nirādhāraṃ vibhāvayan |
svadehaṃ manasi kṣaṇe kṣaṇāt kṣīṇāśayo bhavet || 82 ||
translation: Sitting or lying down, one should contemplate the unsupported, and for a moment focus the mind on one's own body; then the mental tendencies become exhausted.
intent_summary: Contemplate awareness without support while briefly observing the body so that mental tendencies weaken and fall away.
beginner_explanation: Here the instruction is to be still and notice both the open ground of experience and your own body. You are not trying to think hard; you are simply resting with what is there. In that quiet seeing, old mental habits lose their strength.
scholar_explanation: Nirādhāra-vibhāvana evokes the formless substratum, while svadeha-manasi-kṣaṇa directs attention to embodied presence without conceptual proliferation. The verse suggests a twofold move: deconstruct dependence on external supports and then let the body serve as a temporary anchor for disidentification. Kṣīṇāśaya indicates the exhaustion of saṃskāric tendencies through non-grasping awareness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Subtle Body Movement into Peace
sanskrit:
चलासने वस्थतस्याथ शनैिाध देहचालनात् ।
प्रशान्ते मानसे भािे देवि वदव्यौघम् आप्नुयात् ॥ ८३ ॥
transliteration:
calāsane sthitasyātha śanair dehacālanāt |
prāśānte mānase bhāve devi divyaugham āpnuyāt || 83 ||
translation: Or, while seated in a moving posture, by slowly moving the body, O Devi, when the mind-state becomes tranquil, one attains a flood of the divine.
intent_summary: Use gentle bodily motion until the mind becomes peaceful, then allow divine awareness to arise spontaneously.
beginner_explanation: This verse says you do not always need to sit perfectly still. Gentle movement can actually help the mind settle, like rocking a baby to sleep. When the mind becomes calm, a deeper, more sacred feeling can open by itself.
scholar_explanation: Calāsana and dehacālana indicate a kinetic method: controlled movement is used not as distraction but as a means to pacify mānasa-bhāva. Once prāśānta, the practitioner receives divyaugha, the ‘flood’ of divine presence or energy. This reflects the VBT’s willingness to use ordinary bodily dynamics as a gateway to non-ordinary consciousness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Gazing into Clear Space
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
आकाशं विमलं पश्यन्कृत्वा दृवष्टं वनरन्तराम् ।
स्तब्धात्मा तत्क्षणाद्देवि भैरिं िपुराप्नुयात् ॥ ८४ ॥
transliteration:
ākāśaṃ vimalam paśyan kṛtvā dṛṣṭiṃ nirantaram |
stabdhatmā tatkṣaṇād devi bhairavaṃ vapur āpnuyāt || 84 ||
translation: O Devi, gazing continuously at the pure, clear space, with the gaze held uninterrupted and the self-still, one attains the body of Bhairava at once.
intent_summary: Fix the gaze on pure open space until the self becomes motionless and Bhairava-nature is directly realized.
beginner_explanation: Look at open space rather than at objects, and keep your attention steady. As the eyes and mind settle, the usual sense of being a separate observer can stop moving. In that stillness, awareness may feel vast and fearless, like open sky.
scholar_explanation: Ākāśa as vimala is not mere physical sky but a phenomenological openness used for ekāgratā and objectless absorption. Nirantara-dṛṣṭi and stabdhātman denote unbroken visual fixation leading to a halt in self-contraction. The attained ‘Bhairava body’ is the revelation of one’s own non-dual nature as pure presence rather than a literal form.

speaker: Unknown
title: Absorption in the Crown Fire
sanskrit:
लीनं मूवनध वियत्सिधम् भैरित्वेन भाियेत् ।
तत्सिधम् भैरिाकारतेजस्तत्त्वं समाविशेत् ॥ ८५ ॥
transliteration:
līnaṃ mūrdhni viyat-sarvaṃ bhairavatvena bhāvayet |
tat-siddhaṃ bhairavākāra-tejas tattvam āviśet || 85 ||
translation: One should contemplate all the sky dissolved in the crown as Bhairava; by that accomplishment, the essence of luminous Bhairava-form enters one.
intent_summary: Visualize the entire sky gathered into the crown of the head as Bhairava so that luminous identity with that form enters awareness.
beginner_explanation: Imagine all space or sky gathered at the top of your head, full of light and presence. Hold that image steadily until it stops feeling like an imagination and starts feeling like your own awareness. Then the sense of self can open into a radiant, expansive state.
scholar_explanation: This is a crown-center visualization in which viyat-sarva is internalized into mūrdhan and reinterpreted as bhairavatva. The verse moves from bhāvanā to siddhi, then to āviśet, indicating entry into the tattva of luminous identity. It parallels other VBT visualization techniques that collapse external cosmos into a single interior locus.

speaker: Unknown
title: Seeing the World as Bhairava
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
वकवञ्चज्ज्ञातम् द्वैतदावय बाह्यालोकस्तम् पुन् ।
विश्वावद भैरिं रूपं ज्ञात्वानन्तप्रकाशभृत् ॥ ८६ ॥
transliteration:
kiñcij jñātaṃ dvaitadāyi bāhyālokas tam punaḥ |
viśvādi bhairavaṃ rūpaṃ jñātvānantaprakāśa-bhṛt || 86 ||
translation: Whatever is known as giving rise to duality—this outer light and darkness—having known it as the form of Bhairava, beginning with the universe, one becomes filled with infinite light.
intent_summary: Recognize all perceived dualities, including light and darkness, as manifestations of Bhairava and abide as infinite luminosity.
beginner_explanation: The verse invites you to stop dividing the world into spiritual and unspiritual, light and dark. Even what seems ordinary or opposite is seen as part of one sacred reality. When that is clear, awareness feels boundless and bright.
scholar_explanation: The line targets dvaita-dāyi phenomena, especially the apparent split of bāhya-āloka and tamas. By recognizing viśvādi as bhairava-rūpa, the practitioner performs a direct non-dual re-cognition in which all appearance is reabsorbed into ananta-prakāśa. This is a quintessential Kashmir Śaiva move: not rejecting the world, but discerning its identity with consciousness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Dark Moon Contemplation
sanskrit:
एिमेि दुवनधशायां कृष्णपक्षागमे वचरम् ।
तैवमरं भाियन् रूपं भैरिं रूपमेष्यवत ॥ ८७ ॥
transliteration:
evam eva durniśāyāṃ kṛṣṇapakṣāgame ciram |
taimiraṃ bhāvayan rūpaṃ bhairavaṃ rūpam eṣyati || 87 ||
translation: Likewise, during a dark night at the arrival of the dark fortnight, by long contemplating the dark form, one attains the form of Bhairava.
intent_summary: Use darkness and the dark moon as a contemplative support to enter Bhairava-awareness.
beginner_explanation: Instead of resisting darkness, the verse says to use it as a doorway. Sit with the dark, moonless feeling and keep your attention there. The darkness can become a support for a deeper, quieter awareness.
scholar_explanation: Kṛṣṇapakṣāgama and durniśā provide a ritually resonant environment for taimirika-bhāvanā, where darkness functions as a meditative symbol rather than an obstacle. The contemplative object is not mere absence of light but a sādhana on the subtle dark form that reveals Bhairava. The verse reflects tantric valorization of liminal, in-between conditions as gateways to realization.

speaker: Unknown
title: Unclosing the Eyes into Bhairava
sanskrit:
एिमेि वनमील्यादौ नेिे कृष्णाभमाग्रत् ।
प्रसायध भैरिं रूपं भाियम्स्तन्मयो भिेत् ॥ ८८ ॥
transliteration:
evam eva nīmīlyādau netre kṛṣṇābham agrataḥ |
prasārya bhairavaṃ rūpaṃ bhāvayan tanmayo bhavet || 88 ||
translation: Likewise, first half-closing the eyes and then, with a dark-colored point before one, expanding the gaze, by contemplating the form of Bhairava one becomes identified with that.
intent_summary: Use half-closed eyes and a dark focal point to merge into Bhairava's form.
beginner_explanation: This is a simple eye practice: soften the eyes, look toward a dark point, and let your gaze open. As you keep attention there, the boundary between ‘me looking’ and ‘what is seen’ can thin out. The result is a strong feeling of merging with the meditation itself.
scholar_explanation: Nīmīlya and prasārya indicate a controlled ocular rhythm, using kṛṣṇābha-agra as a visual anchor. The practice culminates in tanmaya, ‘becoming that,’ a classic absorption state where dṛśya and draṣṭṛ are no longer experienced as separate. It complements verse 87 by internalizing darkness as a route to Bhairava-identity.

speaker: Unknown
title: Stopping Through Any Sense Gate
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
यस्य कस्येवन्द्रयस्यावप व्याघाताच्च वनरोधत् ।
प्रविष्टस्याद्वये शून्ये तिैिात्मा प्रकाशते ॥ ८९ ॥
transliteration:
yasya kasyendriyasyāpi vyāghātāc ca nirodhataḥ |
praviṣṭasyādvaye śūnye tathaivātmā prakāśate || 89 ||
translation: When any sense is obstructed and restrained, and one has entered the non-dual void, there the Self shines forth.
intent_summary: Use interruption or restraint of any sense faculty as a doorway into non-dual emptiness where the Self reveals itself.
beginner_explanation: If hearing, seeing, or another sense suddenly stops or is deliberately quieted, notice what remains. The empty, open awareness that is left is not blank in a dead way; it is alive. In that openness, your deeper self can become obvious.
scholar_explanation: Vyāghāta of any indriya becomes a nirodha-point, allowing entry into advaya-śūnya. The verse generalizes the method beyond a single sensory channel, making any disruption a sādhana for recognizing the self-luminous ātman. It is an important bridge between sensory withdrawal and non-dual realization in the VBT.

speaker: Unknown
title: A-U-Mless Mantra Opening
sanskrit:
अविन्दुम् अविसगधम् च अकारम् जपतो महान् ।
उदेवत देवि सहसा ज्ञानौघ् परमेश्वर् ॥ ९० ॥
transliteration:
a bindum avisarjaṃ ca akāraṃ japato mahān |
udeti devi sahasā jñānaughaḥ parameśvaraḥ || 90 ||
translation: For the great one who recites a-kāra together with bindu and visarga, O Devi, suddenly there arises a flood of knowledge, the supreme Lord.
intent_summary: Chant or contemplate the subtle phonetic elements of mantra so that a surge of direct knowledge arises.
beginner_explanation: This verse focuses on the smallest parts of mantra, especially the sound ‘a’ and its subtle marks. By resting in these sounds carefully, something deeper can open very quickly. It is like tuning a radio until a clear signal suddenly appears.
scholar_explanation: The verse likely refers to a-mantra contemplation involving a-kāra, bindu, and visarga, the sonic architecture of emergence and return. Jñānaugha and parameśvara indicate an immediate influx of revealed knowing rather than discursive thought. This sits squarely in the VBT’s sound-based dhāraṇā tradition, where phoneme and consciousness are inseparable.

speaker: Unknown
title: Attuning to the End of Sound
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वर्णस्य सविसर्गस्य विसर्गान्तं चेतनं कुरु ।
निराधारेण चित्तेन स्पृशेद्ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ९१ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ |
varṇasya savisargasya visargāntaṃ cetanaṃ kuru |
nirādhāreṇa cittena spṛśed brahma sanātanam || 91 ||
translation: Make your awareness descend to the ending of a letter that has a visarga; with a mind without support, touch the eternal Brahman.
intent_summary: Use the fading tail of a sound as a doorway into unsupported awareness and the timeless ground.
beginner_explanation: Listen closely to the very end of a spoken sound, especially the breathy fade after it. Instead of following the word itself, rest in the tiny gap where the sound is disappearing. That subtle stopping point can open a sense of stillness beyond ordinary thinking.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā uses the visarga-anta of varṇa as an entry into nirādhāra-citta, where attention is placed on the vanishing edge of articulated sound. The practice treats phonemic dissolution as a microcosm of laya, revealing sanātana-brahman through the attenuation of nāda into silence. It resonates with VBT methods that use intervals, endings, and transitions as portals to Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Meditating on the Sky-Like Self
sanskrit:
व्योमाकारं स्वमात्मानम् ध्यायेवद्दवग्भरनािृतम् ।
निराश्रया चित्त् शवि् स्वरूपं दशधयेत्तदा ॥ ९२ ॥
transliteration:
vyomākāraṃ svam ātmānam dhyāyevadvagbharanāiṛtam |
nirāśrayā citta śvi svarūpaṃ daśadhyettadā || 92 ||
translation: Meditate on your own Self as sky-like, filled with the burden of speech; then, when the mind becomes without support, it will perceive its own nature.
intent_summary: Recognize the self as vast and space-like, allowing the mind to become supportless and reveal its own essence.
beginner_explanation: Imagine your true self as open as the sky, not cramped inside the body or thoughts. Let words and mental noise float inside that openness without grabbing them. When the mind stops leaning on anything, you can notice a deeper quiet clarity.
scholar_explanation: The verse presents ātmā as vyomākāra, a sky-like expanse in which vāk or verbality is contained yet not limited. As citta becomes nirāśraya, the practitioner intuits svarūpa-darśana—direct recognition of consciousness as open, unconditioned space. This aligns with śiva-consciousness as ākāśa-like, where boundless awareness is not an object but the medium of all appearances.

speaker: Unknown
title: Piercing Attention into a Small Point
sanskrit:
किंचिदङ्गम् विभिद्यादौ तीक्ष्णसूच्यावदना तत् ।
तथैव चेतनां युक्त्वा भैरवे निर्मला गतिः ॥ ९३ ॥
transliteration:
kiṃcid aṅgaṃ vibhidyādau tīkṣṇa-sūcyāvadānatat |
tathaiva cetanāṃ yuktvā bhairave nirmalā gatiḥ || 93 ||
translation: First, pierce some small part of the body as with a sharp needle; similarly, when consciousness is joined there, there is a stainless movement into Bhairava.
intent_summary: Use sharply focused attention on a small bodily point to enter a pure, Bhairava-like state.
beginner_explanation: Bring your attention to a tiny spot in the body, as if your awareness were a needle touching one exact place. Don’t spread out; stay precise and steady. That very focused attention can become a doorway into a clearer, freer state.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā employs ekāgratā through a minute bodily locus, likened to tīkṣṇa-sūci, to concentrate cetanā into one point. The ‘piercing’ is not merely tactile but an act of concentrated identification in which awareness fuses with the chosen aṅga, yielding nirmalā gati into Bhairava. It exemplifies VBT’s use of the body as an index for non-dual absorption rather than a limiting frame.

speaker: Unknown
title: Nondual Thought Beyond Thought
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वचत्ताद्यन्त्कृवतनाधवस्त ममान्तभाधियेवदवत ।
विकल्पानामभािेन विकल्पैरुवितो भिेत् ॥ ९४ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ |
vcittādyaṃ tyaktvā niḥśvetaṃ mamaṃtābhāṃ ye vadanti |
vikalpānām abhāvena vikalpair udito bhavet || 94 ||
translation: Having abandoned the beginning activity of thought, one should speak of the 'I'-light of mine; by the absence of discursive constructions, one becomes arisen through constructions.
intent_summary: Transcend ordinary thinking by recognizing the subtle source of ‘I’ and letting concepts dissolve into awareness.
beginner_explanation: Notice how thoughts start before they become full stories. Instead of chasing them, look for the simple feeling of ‘I’ or ‘mine’ underneath. When you don’t cling to the story, thought can become a gateway rather than a trap.
scholar_explanation: Despite OCR corruption, the verse points to relinquishing the initial movement of citta and orienting toward ahaṃ/mama-bhāva at a subtler level. The paradox of being ‘arisen through vikalpas by the absence of vikalpas’ indicates that concepts dissolve when their source is recognized as consciousness itself. This is a classic non-dual reversal where thought is not suppressed but seen as self-arising within the unconditioned.

speaker: Unknown
title: Seeing Maya as Unified Activity
sanskrit:
माया विमोवहनी नाम कलाया् कलनं वस्थतम् ।
इत्यावदधमं तत्त्वानां कलयन्न पृथग्भिेत् ॥ ९५ ॥
transliteration:
māyā vimohinī nāma kalayāḥ kalanaṃ sthitam |
ityādidharmaṃ tattvānāṃ kalayan na pṛthag bhavet || 95 ||
translation: Maya, called the deluding one, consists in the activity of differentiation. By discerning the properties beginning with the principles (tattvas) in this way, one does not become separate.
intent_summary: Understand that apparent multiplicity is just the play of differentiation, not true separation.
beginner_explanation: The world can seem broken into many separate things, but this verse says that division itself is part of a larger process. If you see how everything is being mentally labeled and split up, the sense of being cut off loosens. Then the many things can be felt as one unfolding reality.
scholar_explanation: Māyā is described as vimohinī because it operates through kalana, the differentiating activity that superimposes separateness onto the one reality. By examining the tattvas and their dharmas without reifying them, the practitioner does not fall into pṛthaktva, the error of separative perception. The verse is a direct antidote to ontological fragmentation, affirming non-dual discernment within manifestation.

speaker: Unknown
title: Calming Sudden Desire
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
झवगतीच्छां समुत्पन्नामिलोक्य शमं नयेत् ।
यत एि समुद्भूता ततस्तिैि लीयते ॥ ९६ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ |
jhaṭitīcchāṃ samutpannām avalokya śamaṃ nayet |
yata eva samudbhūtā tatas tatraiva līyate || 96 ||
translation: When a sudden desire arises, observe it and bring it to rest; from where it arose, there it is dissolved.
intent_summary: Witness desire as it appears, and let it dissolve back into its own source.
beginner_explanation: When a strong want suddenly appears, don’t immediately obey it or fight it. Just watch it closely and let it settle on its own. Often the feeling fades when it is clearly seen, because it came from the same place it returns to.
scholar_explanation: The verse instructs the practitioner to meet jhaṭitīcchā, a spontaneous impulse, with clear observation and śama. By tracing icchā back to its source, one witnesses the emergence-and-dissolution dynamic of desire as a play of consciousness rather than a personal mandate. This is a subtle laya practice in which affect is neither repressed nor indulged but reabsorbed into its origin.

speaker: Unknown
title: Abiding Where Desire and Knowledge End
sanskrit:
यदा ममेच्छा नोत्पन्ना ज्ञानं िा कस्तदावस्म िै ।
तत्त्वतोऽहम् तथाभूतस्तल्लीनस्तन्मना भिेत् ॥ ९७ ॥
transliteration:
yadā mamecchā no tpanā jñānaṃ vā kas tadā smai vai |
tattvato 'ham tathābhūtas tallīnas tanmanā bhavet || 97 ||
translation: When neither my desire nor knowledge arises, then who am I there? In truth, being thus, one should become absorbed in that and minded as that.
intent_summary: Rest in the state where personal desire and conceptual knowledge are absent, and let identity merge into pure being.
beginner_explanation: There are moments when you don’t feel a personal want, and you’re not busy labeling things. This verse says to notice that gap and ask, ‘Who am I then?’ Instead of answering with ideas, simply rest in that open state.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses the disappearance of icchā and jñāna as a phenomenological cue for entering the non-conceptual field of selfhood. The question ‘ko ’ham?’ is implied as a non-analytic inquiry that turns the practitioner toward tattvataḥ, the real nature beyond egoic activity. Tanmanā and tallīna indicate complete interiorization into the same reality one seeks, a hallmark of the VBT’s recognition-based soteriology.

speaker: Unknown
title: Steadying the Mind in Desire or Knowledge
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
इच्छायामथिा ज्ञाने जाते वचत्तं वनिेशयेत् ।
आत्मिुद्ध्यानन्यचेतास्ततस्तत्त्वाथधदशधनम् ॥ ९८ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ |
icchāyām athavā jñāne jāte cittaṃ niveśayet |
ātmaśuddhyā ananyacetas tatas tattvārthadarśanam || 98 ||
translation: When desire or knowledge has arisen, one should place the mind there; through purification of the Self and with one-pointed consciousness, then comes the seeing of reality.
intent_summary: Use whatever is arising—wanting or knowing—as the very place to stabilize attention and realize truth.
beginner_explanation: If a strong feeling or clear idea appears, don’t see it as a problem. Put your mind there fully and simply, without drifting away. When attention is clean and steady, the deeper truth behind the experience becomes visible.
scholar_explanation: Rather than rejecting icchā or jñāna, the verse recommends entering them with ananyacetas, undivided mind, so that ātma-śuddhi leads to tattvārthadarśana. This reflects the tantric principle that any arising content can function as a śiva-entry point when held without fragmentation. The practice is a discipline of inclusive awareness, not selective suppression.

speaker: Unknown
title: Seeing Knowledge as Groundless
sanskrit:
वनवनधवमत्तं भिेज्ज्ञानम् वनराधारं भ्रमात्मकम् ।
तत्त्वत् कस्यवचन्नैतद् एिम्भािी वशि् वप्रये ॥ ९९ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ |
niviḍhaṃ mittaṃ bhajej jñānaṃ nirādhāraṃ bhramātmakam |
tattvataḥ kasyacin naitat evambhāvī śivaḥ priye || 99 ||
translation: Knowledge appears manifold and groundless, and is delusive in nature; in truth, this does not belong to anyone—thus, O beloved, one becomes Śiva in this way.
intent_summary: See conceptual knowledge as unsupported appearance and recognize the self as Śiva beyond ownership of thought.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that much of what we call knowledge is just a shifting set of ideas with no solid base. If you watch carefully, you may notice that thoughts come and go on their own. Realizing that they are not really ‘mine’ can open a more peaceful way of being.
scholar_explanation: Jñāna is described as nirādhāra and bhramātmaka, emphasizing its constructed, non-self-subsistent character. The crucial insight is de-appropriation: nothing in this play of cognition genuinely belongs to any individual possessor. In this recognition, the practitioner abides as Śiva, the non-possessive ground of all knowing.

speaker: Unknown
title: Perceiving All as Consciousness
sanskrit:
वचद्धमाध सिधदेहेषु विशेषो नावस्त कुिवचत् ।
अतश्च तन्मयं सिं भाियन्भिवजज्जन् ॥ १०० ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantraṃ |
cidbhaṃ dharmaḥ sarvadeheṣu viśeṣo nāsti kutracit |
ataś ca tanmayaṃ sarvaṃ bhāvayan bhajed jñānajan || 100 ||
translation: The nature of consciousness is present in all bodies; there is no difference anywhere. Therefore, by contemplating everything as made of that, one should attain the birth of knowledge.
intent_summary: Contemplate the same consciousness in all beings and things until the sense of difference falls away.
beginner_explanation: Try seeing the same aware presence in every person and in yourself. Outward forms differ, but the living awareness inside is the same. When you keep noticing that, separation starts to soften.
scholar_explanation: The verse states that cid-dharma pervades sarva-deha, negating any ultimate viśeṣa or distinction at the level of consciousness. By bhāvana of sarvaṃ tanmaya, the practitioner cultivates sarvātmatā, the insight that everything is formed of that one conscious reality. This is a direct non-dual contemplative synthesis of doctrine and perception.

speaker: Unknown
title: Purification Through the Storm of Defilements
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
कामक्रोधलोभमोहमदमात्सयधगोचरे ।
िुवद्धं वनवस्तवमतां कृत्वा तत्तत्त्वमिवशष्यते ॥ १०१ ॥
transliteration: vijñānabhairava tantraṃ | kāma-krodha-lobha-moha-mada-mātsarya-dhago-care | buddhaṃ nivastamitaṃ kṛtvā tattatvam avśiṣyate || 101 ||
translation: In the field of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, jealousy, and hatred, make the mind still and quiet; then that reality alone remains.
intent_summary: To see that even amid the strongest afflictive emotions, the mind can be made still so that pure reality reveals itself.
beginner_explanation: This verse says not to wait for a perfect moment. Even when intense feelings like anger, craving, or jealousy are present, you can pause and let the mind settle. When the agitation stops, what remains is the deeper reality beneath the emotion.
scholar_explanation: The verse places samsāra's emotional poisons—kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya—into the field of practice rather than outside it. By 'stilling' the buddhi/mind (nivastamitaṃ kṛtvā), one abides in tattva, the underlying truth, which in VBT terms is Bhairava-consciousness beyond vṛtti and saṃskāra. This is a non-dual method of immediate re-centering in the midst of affective turbulence.

speaker: Unknown
title: Seeing the World as Illusory Display
sanskrit:
इन्द्रजालमयं विश्वं व्यस्तं िा वचिकमधित् ।
भ्रमद्वा ध्यायत् सिं पश्यतश्च सुखोद्गम् ॥ १०२ ॥
transliteration: indrajālamayaṃ viśvaṃ vyastaṃ vā citrakam adhīt | bhramadvā dhyāyāt sarvaṃ paśyataśca sukhodgam || 102 ||
translation: The universe is like a magician's illusion or a painted image; whether dispersed or moving, meditate on it all, and from such seeing there arises joy.
intent_summary: To contemplate the world as a wondrous display rather than a fixed reality, so perception ripens into delight.
beginner_explanation: Here the text asks you to look at the world as if it were a magic show or a painting. Things may seem solid, but they are appearing in a larger field of awareness. When you see them this way, experience becomes lighter and more joyful.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes indrajāla, the classic simile of illusion, and citra/citraka, the painted or displayed universe. The practice is not nihilistic but contemplative: one sees the world's apparent dispersion or motion as a display within consciousness, yielding sukhodgama, the rise of bliss. This aligns with Kashmiri non-dual aesthetics where jagat is a luminous manifestation, not a separate substance.

speaker: Unknown
title: Abiding in the Middle Beyond Pleasure and Pain
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
न वचत्तं वनवक्षपेद् दु्खे न सुखे िा पवरवक्षपेत् ।
भैरवि ज्ञायतां मध्ये वकं तत्त्वमिवशष्यते ॥ १०३ ॥
transliteration: na cittaṃ nikṣipet duḥkhe na sukhe vā parikṣipet | bhairavi jñāyate madhye kiṃ tattvam avśiṣyate || 103 ||
translation: Do not throw the mind into sorrow, nor cast it into pleasure. O Bhairavi, know what remains in the middle—what reality is there?
intent_summary: To remain centered in the gap beyond liking and disliking, and discover the witness that is unchanged.
beginner_explanation: This verse teaches balance. Instead of getting pulled completely into pain or pleasure, stay in the middle and notice what is still present. That quiet presence is deeper than changing moods.
scholar_explanation: The instruction rejects identification with sukha and duḥkha, directing attention to madhya, the interval or center where dualistic oscillation ceases. In VBT, the 'middle' is often a privileged access point to Bhairava-state, because it reveals the conscious knower prior to affective polarization. The verse functions as a practical phenomenology of the witness beyond dvandva.

speaker: Unknown
title: Universal Self Beyond the Body
sanskrit:
विहाय वनजदेहस्थं सिधिास्मीवत भाियन् ।
दृढेन मनसा दृष्ट्या नान्येवक्षण्या सुखी भिेत् ॥ १०४ ॥
transliteration: vihāya nijadehasthaṃ sarvatrāsmīti bhāvayan | dṛḍhena manasā dṛṣṭyā nānyekṣaṇyā sukhī bhavet || 104 ||
translation: Leaving behind the sense of being located only in one's own body, and contemplating, 'I am everywhere,' one becomes happy by a firm mind and vision, not by looking at anything else.
intent_summary: To expand identity beyond the body and rest in the all-pervading self.
beginner_explanation: Instead of feeling trapped inside your body, imagine that your true self is present everywhere. Keep that feeling steady with your mind and sight. This spacious way of seeing brings ease and happiness.
scholar_explanation: The verse shifts from deha-abhiniveśa, fixation on the body, to sarvatrāsmīti-bhāvanā, the contemplative realization 'I am everywhere.' This is a direct application of the expansive aham-vimarśa of Trika, where the self is not limited to embodied location. 'Not seeing another' indicates the collapse of object-oriented seeking into non-dual recognition.

speaker: Unknown
title: Seeing the Hidden Consciousness in Things
sanskrit:
घटादौ यच्च विज्ञानवमच्छाद्यं िा ममान्तरे ।
नैि सिधगतं जातं भाियवन्नवत सिधग् ॥ १०५ ॥
transliteration: ghaṭādau yac ca vijñānam icchādyaṃ vā mamāntare | naiva sarvagataṃ jātaṃ bhāvayan nityavān bhavet || 105 ||
translation: Whatever consciousness is in a pot and other things, or in desire and the like, within me—contemplating that it has never truly become all-pervading, one becomes constant in that awareness.
intent_summary: To perceive consciousness within ordinary objects and inner states, recognizing its unbroken presence.
beginner_explanation: This verse invites you to look for awareness in everyday things, like a pot, and even in your own desires. It says that consciousness is not newly produced; it has always been present. Remembering this helps you stay steady in awareness.
scholar_explanation: The verse asks the practitioner to discern vijñāna in ghaṭa-ādi and in icchā-ādi within oneself, then to see that it is not newly 'made' into sarvagata. The point is that consciousness is not an effect of objects or mental states but their ever-present basis. This supports the Trika view that cit is self-existent and not conditioned by localization.

speaker: Unknown
title: Vigilance in the Subject-Object Relation
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
ग्राह्यग्राहकसवित्त्वं सामान्या सिद्धदेवधनानाम् ।
योगिनां तु विशेषोऽस्ति सम्बन्धे सािधानता ॥ १०६ ॥
transliteration: grāhyagrāhakasattvaṃ sāmānyaṃ siddhadevadhāninām | yogināṃ tu viśeṣo 'sti sambandhe sāva dhānatā || 106 ||
translation: For the accomplished, divine, and blessed, the common fact is the relation of the grasped and the grasper; but for yogins, the special thing is alertness in that relation.
intent_summary: To maintain lucid awareness at the moment consciousness meets an object, instead of falling into automatic duality.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that everyone experiences a knower and a known thing. What makes a yogi different is staying awake right at that meeting point. You don't get lost in the object; you notice the act of knowing itself.
scholar_explanation: Grāhya-grāhaka-sattva is universal, but yogic distinction lies in sambandhe sādhānatā—sustained vigilance within relation itself. This is a subtle epistemic practice: instead of abolishing objects, one holds the interval of cognition so the polarity is recognized as a play of consciousness. It resonates with Trika's emphasis on vimarśa as reflexive awareness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Expanding Into Another's Body
sanskrit:
स्विदन्यशरीरेऽपि सवित्त्वं अनुभावयेत् ।
अपेक्षां स्वशरीरस्य त्यक्त्वा व्यापी भवेत् ॥ १०७ ॥
transliteration: svapadanyaśarīre 'pi sattitvaṃ anubhāvayet | apekṣāṃ svaśarīrasya tyaktvā vyāpī bhavet || 107 ||
translation: One should experience one's own existence even in another's body; abandoning dependence on one's own body, one becomes all-pervading.
intent_summary: To loosen identification with one's own body and realize a wider, universal presence.
beginner_explanation: Try not to think of yourself as trapped inside only this one body. Feel that the same awareness can be present in others too. As that sense deepens, the feeling of being separate begins to open out.
scholar_explanation: The verse extends deha-abhimāna beyond personal embodiment by instructing anubhava of sattva in any other body. By dropping apekṣā on one's own śarīra, one enters vyāpti, all-pervasion, a key Trika notion of expanded selfhood. This practice cultivates non-local identity through empathetic recognition rather than abstract doctrine.

speaker: Unknown
title: Groundless Mind Beyond Thought
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
वनराधारं मन् कृत्वा विकल्पान्न विकल्पयेत् ।
तदात्मपरमात्मत्वे भैरिो मृगलोचने ॥ १०८ ॥
transliteration: nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā vikalpān na vikalpayet | tadātmaparamātmatve bhairavo mṛgalocane || 108 ||
translation: Having made the mind supportless, do not think thoughts upon thoughts. O deer-eyed one, Bhairava is in the identity of the self and the supreme Self.
intent_summary: To let the mind become ungrounded in concepts so that the identity of self and Supreme Self is directly recognized.
beginner_explanation: This verse says to stop propping the mind up with endless thinking. Let it rest without a support, and don't build one thought on top of another. In that quiet, you can recognize that your deepest self is not separate from the highest reality.
scholar_explanation: Nirādhāra-manas marks the collapse of conceptual dependence; vikalpa is to cease producing vikalpa. The verse names the key Trika insight: tad-ātma-paramātmatva, the identity of individual self and Paramātman as Bhairava. The vocative mṛgalocane softens the instruction with devotional intimacy while preserving the radical advaita of the method.

speaker: Unknown
title: Certainty of Identity with the Lord
sanskrit:
सिधज्ञ् सिधकताध च व्यापक् परमेश्वर् ।
स एिाहम् शैिधमाध इवत दार्ढ्ाधवच्छिो भिेत् ॥ १०९ ॥
transliteration: siddhajñānaṃ siddhakartā ca vyāpakaḥ parameśvaraḥ | sa evāhaṃ śaivamārga iti dārḍhyādbhavet śivaḥ || 109 ||
translation: The perfected knower, the perfected doer, the all-pervading Supreme Lord—'He alone am I': by firm conviction in the Shaiva path, one becomes Śiva.
intent_summary: To stabilize the realization that one's own self is identical with the all-pervading Lord.
beginner_explanation: This verse encourages you to become deeply sure that the highest reality is not separate from you. It is not just a passing idea; it should become firm and steady. When that recognition is stable, the text says one becomes like Shiva.
scholar_explanation: The verse equates siddha-jñāna, siddha-kartṛ, and vyāpaka Parameśvara, then culminates in the mahāvākya-like recognition sa evāham. Dārḍhya is essential: the path is not mere intellectual assent but stabilized pratyabhijñā, recognition of one's Śiva-nature. This is explicitly the śaiva mārga of non-dual identity, where the practitioner abides as Śiva through certainty.

speaker: Unknown
title: World as Ripples of Firelight
sanskrit:
जलस्येिोमधयो िह्नेर्ज्ाधलाभङ्ग्य् प्रभा रिे् ।
ममैि भैरिस्यैता विश्वभङ्ग्यो विभेवदता् ॥ ११० ॥
transliteration: jalasyevomayo vahner jvālābhaṅgyaḥ prabhā raveḥ | mamaiva bhairavasyaitā viśvabhaṅgyo vibheditāḥ || 110 ||
translation: As the ripples of water, the tongues of flame, and the rays of the sun are distinctions of one and the same reality, so these diversities of the universe are distinctions of me, Bhairava.
intent_summary: To perceive all variety as the differentiated expression of one Bhairava-consciousness.
beginner_explanation: This verse gives images from water, fire, and the sun to show that many forms can belong to one thing. In the same way, the many forms of the world are not separate from the one reality. Seeing this helps you feel unity beneath diversity.
scholar_explanation: Through analogies of waves, flames, and solar rays, the verse teaches bheda-as-abheda: apparent distinctions are modes of one substance. The universe's viśvabhaṅgī are explicitly identified as Bhairava's own differentiations, not external realities. This is a classic Trika move: diversity is retained phenomenologically but dissolved ontologically into the single luminous agent.

speaker: Unknown
title: Dissolution Through Repeated Falling
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
भ्रान्त्वा भ्रान्त्वा शरीरेण त्ववरतम् भुवि पातनात् ।
क्षोभशविविरामेण परा संजायते दशा ॥ १११ ॥
transliteration:
bhrāntvā bhrāntvā śarīreṇa tv avarataṃ bhuvi pātanāt |
kṣobhāśavi-virāmeṇa parā saṃjāyate daśā || 111 ||
translation: By repeatedly wandering and then, through the body, falling continually to the ground, when agitation comes to rest, the supreme state arises.
intent_summary: Use repeated physical collapse and the settling of agitation to trigger a higher state of consciousness.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a practice where the body is allowed to move, tire, or even collapse until the usual inner restlessness stops. When that agitation drops away, a deeper, quieter state can appear on its own. The key is not force, but letting the body exhaust the momentum of strain.
scholar_explanation: The verse describes a liminal technique in which śārīra-gati and repeated pātana weaken kṣobha, allowing parā daśā to manifest. This resembles a dissolution method: bodily exertion or disorientation is used to interrupt ordinary mental continuity. The phrase kṣobhāśavi-virāmeṇa indicates cessation of agitation as the opening into non-ordinary awareness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Shakti Absorption After Agitation
sanskrit:
आधारेष्वथिाऽशक्त्याऽज्ञानावच्चित्तलयेन िा ।
जातशविसमावेशक्षोभान्ते भैरिं िपु् ॥ ११२ ॥
transliteration:
ādhāreṣv atha śaktyā jñānāvac cittalayena vā |
jātaśakti-samāveśa-kṣobhānte bhairavaṃ vapuh || 112 ||
translation: Then, in the supports, through power (śakti), by means of ignorance or by absorption of mind, when the agitation ends and the power has entered fully, one becomes Bhairava in form.
intent_summary: Let the mind dissolve in its supports until agitation ends and Bhairava-nature shines through.
beginner_explanation: This teaching says that when the mind becomes absorbed and the inner disturbance fades, a more powerful presence can emerge. You can think of it like muddy water settling so that the depth below becomes visible. The verse points to becoming so शांत that your ordinary sense of self is replaced by something vast and vivid.
scholar_explanation: Here the sūtra speaks of ādhāra and śakti-samāveśa, with cittalaya or even jñānāvac (knowledge as veiling/ignorance) functioning as the means by which kṣobha ends. The result is bhairavaṃ vapuh, not as an external deity but as realized identity with Bhairava. It belongs to the set of samāveśa/dissolution techniques in which mentation ceases and one is stabilized in the innate nondual state.

speaker: Unknown
title: Stillness of the Eyes
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सम्प्रदायवममं देवि शृणु सम्यविदाम्यहम् ।
कैवल्यं जायते सद्यो नेत्रयोः स्तब्धमात्रयोः ॥ ११३ ॥
transliteration:
sampradāyam imaṃ devi śṛṇu samyag vadāmy aham |
kaivalyaṃ jāyate sadyo netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayoḥ || 113 ||
translation: Devi, listen to this lineage-teaching: I shall speak it rightly. Liberation (kaivalya) arises immediately when the eyes become perfectly still.
intent_summary: Achieve immediate liberation by fixing the eyes in complete stillness.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that if the eyes become completely still, the mind can fall silent very quickly. Since the eyes often pull attention outward, calming them helps attention turn inward. It is like stopping a spinning top by gently holding it still.
scholar_explanation: Bhairava frames the method as a sampradāya, emphasizing its transmission and efficacy. Netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayoḥ indicates absolute ocular immobility; by suspending the usual outward sensory current, kaivalya arises instantly. The technique aligns with dhāraṇā through sensory arrest and resembles pratyāhāra-like inwardness, yet the text presents it as direct entry into liberation.

speaker: Unknown
title: Silencing Ears and Lower Gate
sanskrit:
सम्कोचं कर्णयोः कृत्वा ह्यधोद्वारे तथैव च ।
अनच्कमहलं ध्यायविशेद्ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ११४ ॥
transliteration:
saṃkocaṃ karṇayoḥ kṛtvā hy adhodvāre tathaiva ca |
anacakam ahaṃ dhyāyann viśed brahma sanātanam || 114 ||
translation: By closing the ears, and likewise the lower opening, meditating on the unlettered ‘I’ (anacka-aham), one enters the eternal Brahman.
intent_summary: Use bodily closure and inward attention on the silent self-sense to enter Brahman.
beginner_explanation: This practice asks you to reduce outside input by closing the ears and guarding the body's lower exit, then rest attention on the wordless sense of 'I am.' By cutting distractions, the mind has less to grasp. The experience can open into a quiet, timeless presence.
scholar_explanation: The instruction combines indriya-saṃkoca with attention to anacka-aham, the phoneme-less अहं, or primordial self-awareness prior to articulated thought. The lower aperture (adhodvāra) closure suggests energetic containment, while the meditation on the unlettered I leads to sanātana brahma. This is a classic interiorization practice where bodily restraint supports recognition of the preconceptual subject.

speaker: Unknown
title: Viewing from the Well
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
कूपावदके महागते वस्थित्वोपरि निरीक्षणात् ।
अविकल्पमते् सम्यक्सद्यवश्चत्तलय् िुटम् ॥ ११५ ॥
transliteration:
kūpāvadake mahāghore vyavasthitvo pari nirīkṣaṇāt |
avikalpam ateḥ samyag sadyaś citta-layaṃ śivam || 115 ||
translation: Standing in a great terrifying pit or well, by looking upward, with thought-free discernment one quickly attains the dissolution of mind into Śiva.
intent_summary: Use a vast or frightening spatial perspective to drop conceptual thinking and let mind dissolve into Śiva.
beginner_explanation: The verse uses the shock of standing in a deep pit and looking up to break ordinary thinking. When the mind cannot maintain its usual stories, it may become quiet and open. This is not about fear for its own sake, but about using a strong visual experience to stop mental chatter.
scholar_explanation: The imagery of kūpa or mahāghora context creates a destabilizing perceptual field; upward gazing becomes a trigger for avikalpa mati. The resulting cittalaya into Śiva reflects the text’s recurring equation of mental cessation with recognition of the absolute. This is another dissolution-by-perception method: spatial extremity induces nonconceptual awareness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Wherever the Mind Wanders
sanskrit:
यि यि मनो यावत िाह्ये िाभ्यन्तरेऽवप िा ।
ति ति वशिािास्था व्यापकत्वात्क्व यास्यवत ॥ ११६ ॥
transliteration:
yatra yatra mano yāti bāhye nābhyantare 'pi vā |
tatra tatra śivatāvasthā vyāpakatvāt kva yāsyati || 116 ||
translation: Wherever the mind goes, whether outside or even inside, there the state of Śiva is present. Because of all-pervadingness, where could it go?
intent_summary: Recognize that whatever appears to the mind is already within the all-pervading Śiva-state.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that there is no place separate from the divine awareness you are seeking. Whether your attention goes outward or inward, the same presence is already there. Realizing this can relax the feeling that you must go somewhere else to find truth.
scholar_explanation: The verse articulates vyāpakatva, the pervasive nature of śivatā-avasthā: no mental movement escapes the field of Śiva. The rhetorical question kva yāsyati denies any real departure of consciousness, since all loci are already pervaded by the same reality. It serves as a direct nondual insight practice, short-circuiting spatial dualism.

speaker: Unknown
title: Mind Dissolves in Each Sense-Path
sanskrit:
यि यिाक्षमागेण चैतन्यं व्यज्यते विभो् ।
तस्य तन्मािधवमधत्वावच्चल्लयाद्भवरतात्मता ॥ ११७ ॥
transliteration:
yatra yatrākṣamārgeṇa caitanyaṃ vyajyate vibhoḥ |
tasya tanmādhyamahattvāc citta-layād bhavatātmatā || 117 ||
translation: Wherever, through any sense-path, consciousness of the Lord becomes manifest, because of the greatness of that middle state, through the dissolution of mind there is one’s own identity with Bhava.
intent_summary: Use any sensory channel as a doorway to the middle state where mind dissolves and one realizes identity with Bhava.
beginner_explanation: Any sense experience can become a doorway if you notice the living awareness behind it. The verse says that the important thing is not the object, but the gap or middle in which awareness is revealed. In that quiet middle, the mind fades and you recognize your deeper self.
scholar_explanation: Akṣamārga here indicates the sensory pathways as legitimate loci of caitanya-vyakti. The tanmādhya, the 'middle' or interval, is emphasized as a significant liminal zone where citta-laya enables bhavatātmatā. This verse bridges sensory perception and nondual realization: the senses are not obstacles but portals when the mind ceases grasping.

speaker: Unknown
title: Awareness in Extremity
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
क्षुताद्यन्ते भये शोके गह्वरे वा रणाद्द्रुते ।
कुतूहलेक्षुधाद्यन्ते ब्रह्मसत्तामयी दशा ॥ ११८ ॥
transliteration:
kṣutādya-ante bhaye śoke gahvare vā raṇād drute |
kutūhalekṣudhādya-ante brahma-sattāmayī daśā || 118 ||
translation: At the end of hunger and the like, in fear, sorrow, a deep cave, or while fleeing from battle—at the end of curiosity and hunger, there is a state made of Brahman’s being.
intent_summary: Use intense extremity, fear, or absorption to reveal a state saturated with Brahman-consciousness.
beginner_explanation: Strong emotions and urgent situations can make the normal mind drop away for a moment. This verse says that in such intense moments, a deeper presence can show itself. Rather than seeking calm only, it points to the hidden opening inside intensity.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā exploits liminal states—bhaya, śoka, guhā, raṇa, kutūhala—where ordinary cognitive structure is destabilized. The result is brahma-sattāmayī daśā, a state suffused with Brahman-being, suggesting that intensity can reveal rather than obscure awareness. It is closely related to other affective and shock-based contemplations in the VBT.

speaker: Unknown
title: Letting Go on Seeing Objects
sanskrit:
वस्तुषु स्मयधमाणेषु दृष्टे देशे मनस् त्यजेत् ।
स्वशरीरं निराधारं कृत्वा प्रसरवत् प्रभुः ॥ ११९ ॥
transliteration:
vastuṣu smaryamāṇeṣu dṛṣṭe deśe manas tyajet |
sva-śarīraṃ nirādhāraṃ kṛtvā prasarat prabhuḥ || 119 ||
translation: When objects are being remembered in a seen place, one should let go of the mind; making one’s own body supportless, the Lord expands forth.
intent_summary: Release mental grasping at the moment of perception so awareness can expand beyond the body.
beginner_explanation: When something appears in front of you, don’t immediately tighten around it with thoughts and labels. Instead, let the mind relax and feel the body as if it had no fixed center. Then awareness can widen, like a room suddenly feeling larger when the furniture is moved away.
scholar_explanation: The verse instructs a deliberate relinquishment of manas at the point of dṛṣṭa-deśa, turning perception into an occasion for de-identification. By rendering the body nirādhāra, the practitioner allows the prabhu, the sovereign awareness, to prasarat. This is a direct contemplative move from object-oriented cognition to expansive subjectless presence.

speaker: Unknown
title: Shining in the Empty Abode
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
क्ववचद्वस्तुवन विन्यस्य शनैदृधवष्टम् वनितधयेत् ।
तज्ज्ञानं वचत्तसवहतं देवि शून्यालयो भिेत् ॥१२० ॥
transliteration:
kvacit vastu viniścitya śanai rūddhāṃ vibhāvayet |
taj jñānaṃ citta-sahitaṃ devi śūnyālayaṃ bhavet || 120 ||
translation: Having fixed on some object, one should slowly contemplate it as restrained; that knowledge, together with the mind, O Devi, becomes an abode of emptiness.
intent_summary: Contemplate an object until it reveals empty space, turning cognition itself into a hollow, spacious abode.
beginner_explanation: This verse suggests looking at something carefully and then seeing that it is not as solid as it first seemed. As attention deepens, the object can become a doorway into spaciousness rather than a thing to cling to. The result is a mind that feels like a clear, open room.
scholar_explanation: The sūtra employs focused vibhāvanā on a selected vastu, then applies a slow constriction or restraint that reveals śūnyālaya. Rather than negating cognition entirely, jñāna-citta itself becomes the locus where emptiness is recognized. This integrates visualization-like attention with śūnyatā imagery within the Tantric nondual framework.

speaker: Unknown
title: Devotion’s Surge Reveals Shakti
sanskrit:
भक्त्युद्रेकावद्वरिस्य यादृशी जायते मवत् ।
सा शवि् शाङ्करी वनत्यं भियेत्तां तत् वशि् ॥ १२१ ॥
transliteration:
bhaktyudrekāvadvarisya yādṛśī jāyate mavat |
sa śaviḥ śāṅkarī vanatyaṃ bhiyettāṃ tat vaśiḥ || 121 ||
translation: Whatever state arises when devotion becomes intense—that Shakti is Śāṅkarī. By that, one should continually become established and controlled by it.
intent_summary: Use intensified devotion as a direct doorway into the living power of Śakti.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that when love or devotion becomes very strong, it reveals a special energy or presence. Instead of treating devotion as just emotion, use it as a way to enter a deeper spiritual state. The instruction is to stay with that intensity and let it lead you inward.
scholar_explanation: Bhaktyudreka here indicates an upsurge of bhakti that manifests as Śāṅkarī-śakti, the power of Śiva itself. The verse treats affective devotion not as a secondary sentiment but as a yogic access point to non-dual recognition, where emotional expansion becomes a form of śakti-sādhana. The practitioner abides in that emergent force until it becomes steady and sovereign.

speaker: Unknown
title: Inner Emptiness Amid Objects
sanskrit:
िस्त्वन्तरे िेद्यमाने सिधिस्तुषु शून्यता ।
तामेि मनसा ध्यात्वा विवदतोऽवप प्रशाम्यवत ॥ १२२ ॥
transliteration:
iṣṭvantare vedyamāne sidhistuṣu śūnyatā |
tāmeva manasā dhyātvā vidito'pi praśāmyati || 122 ||
translation: When emptiness is known amid the known objects and attainments, meditating on that emptiness with the mind, even one who knows becomes शांत, शांत.
intent_summary: Find the empty, spacious ground present within all experiences and rest the mind there.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to the quiet space that can be noticed even while thoughts, objects, or accomplishments are present. If you focus on that sense of openness, the mind settles down. It is like noticing the screen behind the movie images instead of only the images themselves.
scholar_explanation: Śūnyatā is to be apprehended in the midst of viṣaya and siddhi alike, indicating that emptiness is not elsewhere but immanent within phenomena. Meditation on that śūnya reveals a pacifying effect even for the already-informed knower (vidita), aligning with the VBT’s repeated move from objects to the background of awareness-space. The verse echoes the Śaiva non-dual reading of voidness as fullness rather than nihilistic absence.

speaker: Unknown
title: Purity Beyond Purity and Impurity
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
वकंवचज्ज्ञैयाध स्मृता शुवद्ध् सा शुवद्ध् शम्भुदशधने ।
न शुवचह्यधशुवचस्तस्मावन्नविधकल्प् सुखी भिेत् ॥ १२३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava tantram
kiṃcidjñeyā smṛtā śuddhiḥ sā śuddhiḥ śambhudarśane |
na śuciḥ hy aśucis tasmān nirvikalpaḥ sukhī bhavet || 123 ||
translation: In Śambhu’s vision, purity is remembered only as something to be known in some measure; that alone is purity. Since there is, in truth, neither pure nor impure, therefore one should become happily free of thought-construction.
intent_summary: Realize that purity and impurity are conceptual distinctions and rest in thought-free freedom.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that ideas like pure and impure are only partly useful, not ultimate truths. In the deepest view, these labels do not define reality. When you stop clinging to such distinctions, the mind becomes lighter and happier.
scholar_explanation: The verse deconstructs śuddhi/aśuddhi as conceptual constructs relative to śāmbhava-darśana. In the non-dual recognition of Śambhu, moral or ritual purity is subordinated to nirvikalpa awareness, where dualistic classifications cease to bind. This is characteristic of the VBT’s radical interiorization of sādhana into a direct gnosis beyond conventional categories.

speaker: Unknown
title: Bhairava in All Things
sanskrit:
सिधि भैरिो भाि् सामान्येष्ववप गोचर् ।
न च तद्व्यवतरेिेण परोऽस्तीत्यद्वया गवत् ॥ १२४ ॥
transliteration:
sarvaṃ bhairavo bhāvaḥ sāmānyeṣv api gocaraḥ |
na ca tadvyatirekeṇa paro'stīty advayā gatiḥ || 124 ||
translation: Bhairava is the reality of everything; he is accessible even in ordinary things. Apart from that, there is nothing higher—this is the movement of nonduality.
intent_summary: See Bhairava as present in all experience, especially the ordinary, and recognize there is no separate ultimate outside it.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the sacred is not hidden somewhere else; it is present in everyday life. Ordinary experiences can be gateways to the divine. When you realize there is nothing separate from that presence, you begin to see the world in a new way.
scholar_explanation: Sarvaṃ bhairavaḥ asserts the all-pervasiveness of Bhairava as the single substratum of appearances, with sāmānya—common or ordinary phenomena—becoming valid gocara. The second half denies any para distinct from that reality, articulating advaya-gati, the non-dual ‘course’ of realization. This verse is a concise statement of Trika immanence: the transcendent is encountered within the mundane.

speaker: Unknown
title: Equality in Honor and Dishonor
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सम् शिौ च वमिे च समो मानािमानयो् ॥
ब्रह्मण् पवरपूणधत्वावदवत ज्ञात्वा सुखी भिेत् ॥ १२५ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava tantram
samaṃ śatruau ca mitre ca samo mānāvamānayoḥ ||
brahmaṇaḥ paripūrṇatvād iti jñātvā sukhī bhavet || 125 ||
translation: Being equal toward enemy and friend, and equal in honor and dishonor—knowing this to be because Brahman is पूर्ण, complete—one becomes happy.
intent_summary: Cultivate evenness by seeing all opposites as expressions of the fullness of Brahman.
beginner_explanation: This verse advises not to swing wildly between liking and disliking people or between praise and criticism. If you remember that reality is already complete, these opposites lose some of their power over you. That steadiness brings peace.
scholar_explanation: Samatva toward śatru and mitra, māna and avamāna, reflects the Advaitic insight that Brahman’s pūrṇatva leaves no lack to be filled by social validation or rejection. The verse recommends affective equanimity as a symptom and support of non-dual insight. In Kaśmīr Śaivism, this is not indifference but the luminous neutrality of recognized fullness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Freedom from Aversion and Desire
sanskrit:
न द्वेषं भाियेत्क्वावप न रागं भाियेत्क्ववचत् ।
रागद्वेषविवनमुधिौ मध्ये ब्रह्म प्रसपधवत ॥ १२६ ॥
transliteration:
na dveṣaṃ bhāvayet kvāpi na rāgaṃ bhāvayet kvacit |
rāga-dveṣa-vinirmuktau madhye brahma prasarpati || 126 ||
translation: One should not cultivate aversion anywhere, nor desire anywhere. In the middle, free from desire and aversion, Brahman expands forth.
intent_summary: Release craving and rejection so that the middle, peaceful space where Brahman shines can appear.
beginner_explanation: This verse says not to feed strong attraction or strong dislike. When you stop pushing and pulling in that way, a calmer center opens up. In that calm center, a deeper sense of reality becomes visible.
scholar_explanation: Rāga and dveṣa are treated as the polarities that obscure the madhya, the middle, which is a recurrent Tantric access-point. When the practitioner is vinirmukta from these affective distortions, Brahman ‘prasarpati’—spreads or manifests—indicating spontaneous revelation rather than constructed attainment. The verse aligns with Trika’s emphasis on śānta-centered awareness as the locus of revelation.

speaker: Unknown
title: Bhairava as All Experiencability
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
यदिेद्यं यदग्राह्यं यच्छून्यं यदभािगम् ।
तत्सिं भैरिं भाव्यं तदन्ते िोधसम्भि् ॥ १२७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava tantram
yadvedyaṃ yadagrāhyaṃ yac chūnyaṃ yadabhāvagam |
tatsarvaṃ bhairavaṃ bhāvyaṃ tadante bodhasambhavaḥ || 127 ||
translation: Whatever is knowable, whatever is not graspable, whatever is empty, whatever is beyond being—one should contemplate all that as Bhairava; at the end, knowledge arises.
intent_summary: Contemplate all modes of experience and non-experience as Bhairava until direct knowing arises.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to include everything—things you can know, things you cannot grasp, emptiness, and even what seems beyond existence. Instead of separating these into categories, see them all as one divine reality. Doing that can lead to a deeper kind of understanding that is not just intellectual.
scholar_explanation: The verse universalizes bhāvanā by extending Bhairava to vedya, agrāhya, śūnya, and abhāvagata, collapsing epistemic and ontological distinctions. The result is bodhasambhava, the arising of luminous awareness, suggesting that totalized contemplation of all modes of appearing and non-appearing catalyzes recognition. This is a classic VBT strategy of inclusive non-dualization.

speaker: Unknown
title: Enter the Inner Sky
sanskrit:
वनत्ये वनराश्रये शून्ये व्यापके कलनोविते ।
िाह्याकाशे मनः कृत्वा वनराकाशं समाविशेत् ॥ १२८ ॥
transliteration:
nitye nirāśraye śūnye vyāpake kalanojjhite |
bāhyākāśe manaḥ kṛtvā nirākāśaṃ samāviśet || 128 ||
translation: In the eternal, supportless, empty, all-pervading, thought-free [reality], placing the mind in the outer sky, one should enter the skyless [inner expanse].
intent_summary: Use the vastness of external space as a doorway into the even subtler inner no-space of awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse suggests resting the mind on the feeling of open sky. Then, go beyond even that picture of space and notice the boundless openness within. It is like using the horizon to help you notice an even deeper spaciousness inside.
scholar_explanation: The verse moves from bāhyākāśa to nirākāśa, indicating a contemplative transition from imagined external space to the transcendental space of consciousness devoid of spatial limitation. The descriptors nitya, nirāśraya, vyāpaka, and kalanojjhita align this ‘space’ with the unconditioned reality of Śiva consciousness. It closely parallels other akāśa and śūnya dhāraṇās in the VBT.

speaker: Unknown
title: Let the Mind Become Wave-Free
sanskrit:
यि यि मनो यावत तत्तत् तेनैि तत्क्षणम् ।
