पवरत्यज्यानिवस्थत्या वनस्तरङ्गस्ततो भिेत् ॥ १२९ ॥
transliteration:
yatra yatra mano yāti tattat tenaiva tatkṣaṇam |
parityajyānavasthitayā nistaraṅgas tato bhavet || 129 ||
translation: Wherever the mind goes, there indeed, at that very moment, [it should be] abandoned; by remaining unestablished, one then becomes wave-less.
intent_summary: Stop following the mind’s movements so it can settle into a still, wave-free state.
beginner_explanation: This verse teaches a simple practice: whenever your mind runs to something, notice it and let it go immediately. Don’t build a home in any thought. Over time, the mind becomes calmer, like water with no ripples.
scholar_explanation: The instruction is a form of immediate pratyavamarśa: every movement of manas is recognized and relinquished, producing nistaraṅga, wave-less stillness. This is less suppression than non-abidance in transient mental forms, allowing the practitioner to repose in the background awareness that is not moved by thought. It resonates with dhāraṇās of kṣaṇa, madhya, and mental cessation throughout the text.

speaker: Unknown
title: Repeat the Name of Bhairava
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
भया सिधम् रियवत सिधदो व्यापकोऽवखले ।
इवत भैरिशब्दस्य सन्ततोच्चारणावच्छि् ॥ १३० ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava tantram
bhayaṃ sarvaṃ harati sarvado vyāpako'khile |
iti bhairavaśabdasya santato_ccāraṇāvacchinnaḥ || 130 ||
translation: [He] removes all fear, gives all, and pervades all. Thus, one should be uninterruptedly engaged in the utterance of the word ‘Bhairava.’
intent_summary: Use continual repetition of the word Bhairava to dissolve fear and invoke pervasive divine presence.
beginner_explanation: This verse recommends repeating the word “Bhairava” again and again. The repetition helps replace fear with a sense of protection and vastness. The sound itself becomes a way to remember the divine presence everywhere.
scholar_explanation: The verse assigns mantra-like efficacy to the śabda ‘Bhairava,’ whose semantic field—bhaya-haraṇa, sarva-dāna, vyāpti—mirrors the deity’s salvific and all-pervasive nature. Santata-ucāraṇa supports mantra-abhyāsa as a sonic upāya, likely functioning through continuous recollection until the name and named converge. It belongs to the VBT’s sound-based approaches where recitation stabilizes recognition.

speaker: Unknown
title: Dissolving the Sense of 'I' and 'Mine'
sanskrit:
अहं ममेदवमत्यावद प्रवतपवत्तप्रसङ्गत् ।
वनराधारे मनो यावत तद्ध्यानप्रेरणाच्छमी ॥ १३१ ॥
transliteration:
ahaṃ mamedam avamatyāvād pravṛttapravattiprasaṅgāt |
vanarādhāre mano yāvat tad-dhyāna-preraṇāc chamī || 131 ||
translation: By setting aside the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and by the arising and ceasing of mental activity, until the mind, resting on the support of the forest, becomes quiet through the impulse of that meditation. || 131 ||
intent_summary: The verse teaches the practitioner to let possessive self-referential thinking subside so the mind can grow still in meditation.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to the way our minds keep saying “me” and “mine,” which creates constant movement. The practice is to notice that habit and let it soften. When that grip loosens, the mind can settle into quietness.
scholar_explanation: The verse targets ahaṃkāra and mamakāra, the egoic constructions of self and possession, and recommends their deactivation through repeated contemplative settling. The imagery of the mind resting in a 'forest-support' (vanādhāra / vanarādhāra in the OCR) suggests withdrawal from structured conceptual support into an unconditioned contemplative field. This aligns with VBT methods that dissolve vikalpa and allow dhyāna to generate śamī, inner pacification.

speaker: Unknown
title: Meditating on Omnipresent Support
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
वनत्यो विभुवनधराधारो व्यापकश्चावखलावधप् ।
शब्दान्प्रवतक्षणं ध्यायन्कृताथोऽथाधनुरूपत् ॥ १३२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantra |
vanatyo vibhvavubhavadharādhāro vyāpakaś cāvakhilāvadhp |
śabdān pravat kṣaṇaṃ dhyāyan kṛtārtho 'thādhanu rūpat || 132 ||
translation: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra. The one who has the support of the world, who pervades all and is beyond all limits, becomes accomplished by meditating for a moment on sounds as they arise, in the form of the bow. || 132 ||
intent_summary: The verse instructs one to contemplate the all-pervading, boundaryless nature of reality while attending to sound as it appears and vanishes.
beginner_explanation: Here the practice is to sense that reality is not boxed in anywhere. You listen to sound as it comes and goes, and let that remind you of something vast and open. In that openness, the sense of being limited can drop away.
scholar_explanation: Despite OCR corruption, the verse clearly evokes Bhairava as vibhvav, dharādhāra, and vyāpaka—support of all, pervading, and beyond limits—while using śabda as a contemplative support. The phrase 'adhanu-rūpat' likely points to a bow-like form, a standard Tantric metaphor for focused one-pointedness or the arc of attention. The teaching is to use transitory sound as a doorway into the limitless dhruva or vyoman-like ground.

speaker: Unknown
title: Seeing the World as Magical Appearance
sanskrit:
अतत्त्ववमन्द्रजालाभवमदं सिधमिवस्थतम् ।
वकं तत्त्ववमन्द्रजालस्य इवत दार्ढ्ाधच्छमं व्रजेत् ॥ १३३ ॥
transliteration:
atattvam antrajālābhavaṃ madaṃ siddham ivāsthitam |
kvaṃ tattvam antrajālasya iti dārḍhyāc chamāṃ vrajet || 133 ||
translation: Seeing the world as not-That, like a magical net or illusion, and established as if accomplished, one should ask: 'Where is the reality of this net of illusion?' In this way one reaches firmness and peace. || 133 ||
intent_summary: The verse asks the practitioner to recognize appearances as illusory display and to stabilize in the insight that they lack independent reality.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the world can be seen like a magic trick: vivid, but not solid in the way it seems. Instead of getting caught in appearances, ask where their fixed reality actually is. That questioning can bring a deep sense of peace.
scholar_explanation: The verse employs māyā-like imagery—'indra-jāla'—to undermine the solidity of phenomena and to point toward atattva, the absence of independently existing essence. The rhetorical question 'where is the tattva of this net?' functions as vicāra that culminates in dārḍhya and śama. This is a classic nondual strategy in the VBT: re-cognize appearance as display (ābhāsa) rather than binding reality.

speaker: Unknown
title: World as Void of Independent Being
sanskrit:
आत्मनो वनविधकारस्य क्व ज्ञानं क्व च िा वक्रया ।
ज्ञानायत्ता िवहभाधिा अत् शून्यवमदं जगत् ॥ १३४ ॥
transliteration:
ātmano 'nuvidhakārasya kva jñānaṃ kva ca vā kriyā |
jñānāyattā vibhāvaḥ āḥ śūnyam idaṃ jagat || 134 ||
translation: For the Self, which is of many forms, where is knowledge and where indeed is action? Since manifestation depends on knowing, this world is empty. || 134 ||
intent_summary: The verse directs one to see that knowledge, action, and the world itself are empty of separate existence when viewed from the Self.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to look for separate “knowing” and “doing” in the deepest Self and not find them there. If everything depends on consciousness, then the world is not a solid thing standing apart from it. Seeing that can loosen attachment to ordinary reality.
scholar_explanation: The OCR is rough, but the doctrinal point is clear: the ātman is presented as multiform yet prior to the duality of jñāna and kriyā. Because manifestations (vibhāva) are said to depend on cognition, the universe is declared śūnya—not nihilistically, but empty of independent, self-standing essence. This resonates with Śaiva idealism: all objects are dependent ābhāsa within consciousness.

speaker: Unknown
title: Beyond Bondage and Liberation
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
न मे बन्धो न मोक्षो मे भीतस्यैता विभीषिकाः ।
प्रवर्तविम्बवमदम् शुद्धेजडरेष्विव विवस्वत् ॥ १३५ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantra |
na me bandho na mokṣo me bhītasyaitā vibhīṣikāḥ |
pravṛttibimbam idam śuddhe jaḍareṣv iva vivasvat || 135 ||
translation: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra. For me there is no bondage, and no liberation either; these are terrors for the fearful. This is a reflected appearance of activity, like the sun in pure inanimate things. || 135 ||
intent_summary: The verse teaches the practitioner to rest in the reality beyond the opposites of bondage and liberation.
beginner_explanation: Here the teaching is that the deepest truth is beyond both being trapped and being freed. Those ideas matter when you are afraid, but not at the level of pure awareness. The verse asks you to see life’s movements as reflections rather than ultimate facts.
scholar_explanation: This is a direct statement of nondual Śaiva siddhānta in the broad sense: bandha and mokṣa are constructs operative only for the bhīta, the frightened subject bound to dualistic identification. The comparison to the sun reflected in pure inert things (śuddhe jaḍa-reṣv iva vivasvat) suggests that bondage/liberation are appearances within consciousness, not modifications of consciousness itself. It is a classic closure to the dhāraṇā sequence, reasserting the immutable bhairava-state.

speaker: Unknown
title: Withdrawing from the Senses
sanskrit:
इन्द्रियद्वारकं सर्वं सुखदुःखावदसम्गमम् ।
इतीन्द्रियाणि सम्त्यज्य स्वस्थः स्वात्मनि वर्तते ॥ १३६ ॥
transliteration:
indriya-dvāraṃ sarvaṃ sukha-duḥkhādi-saṃgamam |
ity indriyāṇi santyajya svasthaḥ svātmani vartate || 136 ||
translation: Everything enters through the gates of the senses and meets with pleasure, pain, and so on. Therefore, having set the senses aside, one remains established in one's own Self. || 136 ||
intent_summary: The verse instructs the practitioner to withdraw from sensory engagement and abide in the Self.
beginner_explanation: Our senses constantly pull us outward with pleasures and pains. This verse suggests stepping back from that stream for a moment. When the senses quiet down, you can feel more settled in yourself.
scholar_explanation: The senses are described as indriya-dvāra, the 'gates' through which sukha-duḥkha and other opposites are experienced. The prescribed move is indriya-saṃtyāga, not necessarily physical suppression but a relinquishment of outwardly bound attention. The result is svastha, 'resting in oneself,' a central contemplative aim across Tantric and Vedāntic traditions.

speaker: Unknown
title: Seeing Knowledge and Known as One Light
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
ज्ञानप्रकाशकं सर्वेणात्मा प्रकाशकः ।
एकवमकस्वभावत्वात्ज्ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं विभाव्यते ॥ १३७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantra |
jñāna-prakāśakaṃ sarvaṃ ātmā prakāśakaḥ |
ekatmika-svabhāvatvāj jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ vibhāvyate || 137 ||
translation: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra. The Self illuminates everything that illuminates knowledge; because of the single-natured essence, knowledge and the known are contemplated as one. || 137 ||
intent_summary: The verse teaches the practitioner to recognize that knowing and the known arise from one self-luminous awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that awareness is what lets everything be known at all. Instead of seeing a split between the knower and the thing known, look for the single light that makes both possible. That can feel like realizing the screen on which a movie appears, not just the movie itself.
scholar_explanation: The verse articulates a key pratyabhijñā insight: ātmā is prakāśaka of all jñāna-prakāśana, and due to ekātmika-svabhāva, jñāna and jñeya are to be contemplated as non-different. This collapses epistemic duality into one luminous consciousness, echoing Kashmir Śaivism's doctrine of prakāśa-vimarśa unity. The contemplative move is not mere philosophy but a direct re-seeing of cognition as self-revelation.

speaker: Unknown
title: The Fourfold One as Bhairava Body
sanskrit:
मानसं चेतना शक्तिरात्मा चेति चतुष्टयम् ।
यदा प्रिये पवरक्षीणं तदा तद्भैरवं वपुः ॥ १३८ ॥
transliteration:
mānasaṃ cetanā śaktir ātmā ceti catuṣṭayam |
yadā priye parikṣīṇaṃ tadā tad bhairavaṃ vapuḥ || 138 ||
translation: Mind, consciousness, power (śakti), and Self: when this fourfold division is exhausted, beloved one, then that is the body of Bhairava. || 138 ||
intent_summary: The verse teaches that when all inner distinctions collapse, the practitioner realizes Bhairava's own nature.
beginner_explanation: We usually divide ourselves into parts: mind, awareness, energy, and self. This verse says that when those divisions lose their force, what remains is not emptiness but a deeper wholeness. That wholeness is called Bhairava.
scholar_explanation: The catuṣṭaya of mānasa, cetanā, śakti, and ātmā functions as a phenomenological map of divided subjectivity. When parikṣīṇa—thoroughly attenuated or exhausted—these distinctions no longer structure experience, revealing bhairava-vapuḥ, the embodied form of the Absolute. This is an explicit collapse of psychological and metaphysical differentiation into nondual identity.

speaker: Unknown
title: One Hundred Twelve Teachings Complete
sanskrit:
वनस्तरङ्गोपदेशानां शतमुक्तं समासत् ।
द्वादशाभ्यवधकं देवि यज्ज्ञात्वा ज्ञानविज्जन् ॥ १३९ ॥
transliteration:
niṣṭaraṅgopadeśānāṃ śatam uktaṃ samāsataḥ |
dvādaśābhyadhikaṃ devi yaj jñātvā jñānavit || 139 ||
translation: Thus, O Goddess, a hundred teachings have been briefly stated; knowing the twelve beyond that, one becomes a knower of knowledge. || 139 ||
intent_summary: The verse marks the completion of the instruction set and gestures toward mastery through understanding the remaining teachings.
beginner_explanation: This verse is like the teacher saying, “I’ve given you the main body of the instructions.” It hints that there are more to be understood to complete the full method. The point is to recognize the teaching as a complete path.
scholar_explanation: Although OCR is uncertain, the verse clearly summarizes the set as niṣṭharaṅga upadeśa, a compact wave-less instruction corpus, and refers to the totality of the 112 plus the concluding dozen or so. It functions as a meta-verse, signaling completion of the dhāraṇā sequence and affirming that true jñānavit is one who comprehends the whole integrated vision. The numeral wording is preserved as a textual marker rather than a strict arithmetical claim.

speaker: Unknown
title: The Yoked One Becomes Bhairava
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अि चैकतमे युिो जायते भैरवः स्वयम् ।
वाचा करोति कर्माणि शापानुग्रहकारकः ॥ १४० ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantra |
api caikatame yukto jāyate bhairavaḥ svayam |
vācā karoti karmāṇi śāpānugrahakārakaḥ || 140 ||
translation: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra. And when united in the one, Bhairava himself arises; by speech he performs actions, bringing about curse and grace. || 140 ||
intent_summary: The verse teaches that union in the one reality awakens Bhairava's spontaneous power in speech and action.
beginner_explanation: When someone is fully settled in the deepest unity, their words and actions become powerful and spontaneous. The verse says this state is not about personal ego but about Bhairava arising directly. Such a person can affect others strongly, for good or ill.
scholar_explanation: The verse states that in ekatama-yoga or ekatame yukta, Bhairava svayam manifests, indicating identity with the Absolute rather than devotional proximity. Speech (vāc) becomes an instrument of karmāṇi and of śāpa-anugraha, the polar powers of cursing and blessing, reflecting śakti's autonomous efficacy. This is a sign of siddhi arising from nondual realization, though the text's emphasis remains on recognition rather than occult power.

speaker: Unknown
title: Immortality and Siddhi of the Attained One
sanskrit:
अजरामरतामेति सोऽणिमादिगुणान्वित् ।
योगिनीनां प्रियो देवि सिद्धमेलापकाधिपः ॥ १४१ ॥
transliteration:
ajarāmaratām eti so'ṇimādi-guṇānvitaḥ |
yoginīnāṃ priyaḥ devi siddha-melāpakādhipaḥ || 141 ||
translation: He attains deathlessness and immortality, endowed with powers such as minuteness (aṇimā). O Devi, he is dear to the yoginīs and the lord of the gathering of the perfected ones.
intent_summary: This verse praises the liberated adept as one who has transcended mortality and attained powers, recognition among yoginis, and mastery in the assembly of siddhas.
beginner_explanation: The verse says that when practice is fully accomplished, a person is no longer bound by ordinary fear of death. Such a person is also described in the language of yogic powers and spiritual honor. It is a praise of the accomplished state rather than a method to do.
scholar_explanation: The verse belongs to the concluding eulogy of the siddha, describing one who attains ajaramaratā, deathlessness, together with aṇimādi-guṇa, the set of yogic attainments. The references to yoginī and siddha-melāpaka indicate tantric belonging and authority within the non-dual community. The emphasis is on fruition: realization manifests as freedom from decay and social-spiritual sovereignty among realized beings.

speaker: Unknown
title: Devi Questions the Scope of Teaching
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
जीन्नवप विमुक्तोऽसौ कुर्वन्नवप न वलप्यते ।
श्री देवी उवाच ।
इदं यवद विपुदेव परायाश्च महेश्वर ॥ १४२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava-tantram
jīnnava pa vimukto'sau kurvannava pa na valapyate |
śrī devī uvāca |
idaṃ yavad vipudeva parāyāś ca maheśvara || 142 ||
translation: He is free and does not lament, even while acting. Then Śrī Devī said: O great Lord, to what extent does this, O divine one, belong to the supreme reality?
intent_summary: Devi asks how liberation and action can coexist, and seeks clarification about the relation between practice, action, and the supreme state.
beginner_explanation: Here Devi is basically asking: if a person is free, do they still act like everyone else? And if so, what makes that freedom real? This is the kind of question people ask when they want to know how spiritual life fits with ordinary life.
scholar_explanation: The verse introduces a doctrinal inquiry into jīvanmukti and action: the liberated one (vimukta) continues to function without lamentation or bondage. Devi’s question probes the extension of this condition into parā, the supreme plane, raising the issue of how sahaja freedom appears within embodied activity. The OCR is damaged, but the core dialogical intention is clear: she requests clarification of the scope of Brahmanical/Tantric realization in relation to conduct.

speaker: Unknown
title: Who Performs Japa and Worship?
sanskrit:
एवमुिव्यवस्थायां जप्यते को जपश्च कः ।
ध्यायते को महानाथ पूज्यते कश्च तृप्यति ॥ १४३ ॥
transliteration:
evam uktvā vyavasthāyāṃ japyate ko japaś ca kaḥ |
dhyāyate ko mahānātha pūjyate kaś ca tṛpyati || 143 ||
translation: Having said this, in such an order, who is it that recites japa, and who is the japa itself? O great Lord, who meditates, who is worshiped, and who is satisfied?
intent_summary: Devi asks who the real agent is in mantra, meditation, worship, and fulfillment when nonduality is taken seriously.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks a deep question: if everything is really one, then who is doing the spiritual practice? Who is praying, who is meditating, and who is receiving the prayer? It challenges the ordinary idea that there is a separate person doing things to reach God.
scholar_explanation: The inquiry deconstructs ritual agency by asking who performs japa, dhyāna, pūjā, and who experiences tṛpti. In a non-dual framework, subject, act, and object are all provisional designations; the question tests whether ritual can be understood as self-recognition rather than dualistic transaction. This is a classic move in Śaiva Tantra, where practice is re-read through the lens of abheda.

speaker: Unknown
title: Bhairava Explains Outer Practice
sanskrit:
हूयते कस्य वा होमो यागः कस्य च किं कथम् ।
श्री भैरव उवाच ।
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
एषाि प्रवक्रया िाह्या स्थूलेष्वेि मृगेक्षणे ॥ १४४ ॥
transliteration:
hūyate kasya vā homo yāgaḥ kasya ca kiṃ katham |
śrī bhairava uvāca |
vijñānabhairava-tantram
eṣā hi prakriyā bāhyā sthūleṣv eva mṛgekṣaṇe || 144 ||
translation: For whom, and how, is oblation made? For whom is the sacrifice performed? Śrī Bhairava said: O deer-eyed one, this is indeed an outer procedure, operating only in gross things.
intent_summary: Bhairava distinguishes external ritual acts from the higher inner realization that the tantra points toward.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava answers that offerings and sacrifices belong to outer ritual. These are not the deepest level of the teaching. The real point is to move from external actions to an inner understanding.
scholar_explanation: Bhairava classifies homo and yāga as bāhya-prakriyā, external procedures that pertain to sthūla, gross forms. The verse functions as a hermeneutic pivot: ritual is not denied, but subordinated to the subtle, internalized soteriology of VBT. The address mṛgekṣaṇe is the standard affectionate epithet for Devi, preserving the dialogical frame.

speaker: Unknown
title: Japa as the Self-Radiant Inner Sound
sanskrit:
भूयो भूय् परे भािे भािना भाव्यते वह या ।
जप् सोऽि स्वयं नादो मन्त्रात्मा जप्य ईदृश् ॥ १४५ ॥
transliteration:
bhūyo bhūyaḥ pare bhāve bhāvanā bhāvyate yayā |
japaḥ so'sau svayaṃ nādo mantrātmā japy īdṛśaḥ || 145 ||
translation: Again and again, that contemplation by which the supreme state is cultivated—that very japa is itself the spontaneous inner sound, the essence of mantra; japa is of this kind.
intent_summary: This verse teaches that true japa is not mere verbal repetition but repeated interior dwelling in the supreme state as living inner sound.
beginner_explanation: Instead of just saying a mantra out loud, this verse points to a deeper kind of repetition inside the mind and heart. The mantra becomes something like an inner music or current that keeps returning on its own. The practice is to rest in that living sense of presence.
scholar_explanation: Japa is redefined as bhāvanā of the parā-bhāva, repeated cultivation of the supreme condition until it ripens as svayaṃ-nāda. The equation of mantra with inner resonance reflects Tantric theories in which mantra is not merely phonetic but a self-revealing vibration of consciousness. This verse links mantra practice to subtle sound (nāda) and to internalization beyond spoken recitation.

speaker: Unknown
title: Meditation Beyond Form and Support
sanskrit:
ध्यानं वह वनश्चला िुवद्धवनधराकारा वनराश्रया ।
न तु ध्यानं शरीरावक्षमुखहस्तावदकल्पना ॥ १४६ ॥
transliteration:
dhyānaṃ hi niścalā buddhir nirākārā nirāśrayā |
na tu dhyānaṃ śarīrākṣa-mukha-hastādi-kalpanā || 146 ||
translation: Meditation is a steady intellect, formless and without support; meditation is not the imagination of the body, eyes, face, hands, and so on.
intent_summary: This verse defines real meditation as stable, formless awareness rather than mental imagery of body parts or shapes.
beginner_explanation: True meditation is described here as calm, steady attention that does not cling to images. It is not about picturing bodies, faces, or hands in the mind. The point is to rest in a clear, simple awareness.
scholar_explanation: Dhyāna is identified with niścalā buddhi, a steady mind, and characterized as nirākāra and nirāśraya. The verse rejects imagistic conceptualization (kalpanā) of bodily forms as the essence of meditation, thereby privileging non-objectifying awareness. This resonates with VBT’s broader movement from supported contemplation to direct recognition of consciousness itself.

speaker: Unknown
title: Puja in the Great Void
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
पूजा नाम न पुष्पाद्यैर्यथा मवत्यते दृढा ।
वनविधकल्पे महाव्योमि सा पूजा ह्यद्राल्लयः ॥ १४७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava-tantram
pūjā nāma na puṣpādyair yathā matyeta dṛḍhā |
nirvikalpe mahāvyome sā pūjā hy adralayaḥ || 147 ||
translation: Worship is not, as is commonly thought, by flowers and the like. In the unconditioned great expanse, that is worship indeed, the firm dissolution into the undivided great space.
intent_summary: This verse teaches that genuine worship is absorption in nonconceptual vastness, not merely external offerings.
beginner_explanation: Worship is usually thought of as offering flowers or other objects. This verse says the real offering is inward: resting in a vast, open awareness with no extra thoughts. It is like letting the mind dissolve into open sky.
scholar_explanation: Pūjā is reinterpreted as abiding in nirvikalpa mahāvyoma, the great space of undivided consciousness. The verse explicitly contrasts ritual paraphernalia with internal laya, suggesting that true offering is the dissolution of constructed duality into spacious awareness. The term adralaya points to a settled merging, making worship identical with contemplative absorption.

speaker: Unknown
title: Satisfaction in the Many and the One
sanskrit:
अनेकतमयुविस्थे योत्पद्येत वदनावद्दनम् ।
भवरताकारता साऽव तृप्तिरत्यन्तपूर्णता ॥ १४८ ॥
transliteration:
anekatama-yugyasthé yotpadyeta dinād dinam |
bharitākāratā sā ca tṛptir atyanta-pūrṇatā || 148 ||
translation: From whatever condition arises day after day, there is that fullness of being filled; that is satisfaction, that is utter completeness.
intent_summary: This verse points to an ever-renewing fullness that can arise in any circumstance when one abides in nondual completeness.
beginner_explanation: The verse says that true contentment does not depend on a special situation. Even as life changes from day to day, one can feel an inner fullness that keeps filling everything. It is a steady sense of being complete.
scholar_explanation: The verse speaks of bharitākāratā, the condition of being pervaded or filled, as tṛpti and atyanta-pūrṇatā. While the OCR is corrupt, the practical point is clear: in the flow of varied circumstances, the practitioner recognizes fullness as intrinsic, not contingent. This is a phenomenology of nondual sufficiency, where ordinary experience is transmuted into plenitude.

speaker: Unknown
title: Mind-Offering in the Great Void Fire
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
महाशून्यालये िह्नौ भूताक्षविषयावदकम् ।
हूयते मनसा साधं स होमश्चेतनास्रुचा ॥ १४९ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava-tantram
mahāśūnyālaye vahniṃ bhūtākṣa-viṣayādikam |
hūyate manasā sārdhaṃ sa homo cetanā-srucā || 149 ||
translation: In the abode of great emptiness, the elements, senses, and objects are offered into the fire together with the mind; this is the oblation, with consciousness as the ladle.
intent_summary: The verse teaches an internal sacrifice in which all experience is mentally offered into the fire of awareness, dissolving duality.
beginner_explanation: Imagine placing everything you experience—your body, senses, thoughts, and objects—into a sacred fire inside awareness. That inner giving-up is the real sacrifice here. Consciousness itself is the tool that makes the offering.
scholar_explanation: This verse internalizes homo as a meditative offering into mahāśūnyālaya, the dwelling-place of great void or openness. Bhūta, indriya, and viṣaya are dissolved together with manas, while cetanā functions as the sruc, the ritual ladle, signifying that consciousness itself performs the transmutation. The imagery strongly aligns with Tantric laya and the sacrificial re-reading of ordinary cognition.

speaker: Unknown
title: Supreme Sacrifice of Bliss
sanskrit:
यागोऽि परमेशावन तुवष्टरनन्दलक्षणा ।
क्षपणात्सिधपापानां िाणात्सिधस्य पािधवत ॥ १५० ॥
transliteration:
yāgo'sau parameśāni tuṣṭir ānandalakṣaṇā |
kṣapaṇāt sarva-pāpānāṃ pālanaāt sarvasya pārvati || 150 ||
translation: That sacrifice, O Supreme Goddess, is satisfaction characterized by bliss; by the destruction of all sins and the protection of all, O Pārvatī.
intent_summary: This verse defines the highest sacrifice as the blissful satisfaction that destroys impurity and protects the practitioner.
beginner_explanation: Here the teacher says the highest sacrifice is not about external fire or objects. It is a state of deep happiness and inner contentment that clears away old burdens. It is also described as protective and purifying.
scholar_explanation: Yāga is identified with tuṣṭi and ānanda-lakṣaṇa, making sacrifice a phenomenology of fulfilled consciousness rather than an external rite. The verse claims purificatory power—kṣapaṇa of pāpa—and protective efficacy, which in Śaiva terms reflects the liberating and safeguarding nature of realization. The devotionally charged address to Pārvatī preserves the liturgical frame while collapsing ritual into blissful nondual fruition.

speaker: Unknown
title: Bhairava-Identity as the Sacred Field
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
रुद्रशविसमावेशस्तत् क्षेत्रं भावना परा ।
अन्यथा तस्य तत्त्वस्य का पूजा काश्च तृप्यवत ॥ १५१ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
rudraśivasamāveśas tat kṣetraṃ bhāvanā parā |
anyathā tasya tattvasya kā pūjā kāś ca tṛpyavāt || 151 ||
translation: The absorption into Rudra-Śiva is the supreme field of contemplation. Otherwise, what worship could there be for that Reality, and what offering could satisfy it?
intent_summary: To teach that realizing Bhairava through inner absorption is the true sacred act, beyond external worship.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the deepest worship is not done with objects, but by entering fully into the reality of Bhairava through awareness. If you already know the Divine as your own essence, external rituals are secondary. It is like recognizing the sun in the sky rather than trying to honor it by lighting a lamp.
scholar_explanation: The term samāveśa points to complete immersion or identity with Rudra-Śiva, and bhāvanā parā indicates the highest contemplative act. The verse rejects the adequacy of external pūjā for one who has realized tattva, since the absolute is not an object to be propitiated. This aligns with the VBT's nondual orientation where recognition (pratyabhijñā) supersedes ritual dualism.

speaker: Unknown
title: Inner Immersion in One's Own Self
sanskrit:
स्वतन्त्रानन्दविज्ञानसारः स्वात्मा हि सिद्धः ।
आवेशनं तत्स्वरूपे स्वात्मन् स्नानमीवरतम् ॥ १५२ ॥
transliteration:
svatantrānandavijñānasāraḥ svātmā hi siddhaḥ |
āveśanaṃ tat-svarūpe svātman snānam īvaratam || 152 ||
translation: One's own Self is indeed established as the essence of independent blissful consciousness. Entry into that own form is the supreme bath in the Self.
intent_summary: To direct the practitioner to merge into the already complete self-luminous Self as the highest purification.
beginner_explanation: This verse says you do not need to go anywhere to find the deepest truth; it is already present as your own Self. To 'bathe' in it means to let your attention sink into that inner presence until it feels completely natural. Think of it as returning home and washing away distraction by simply resting as yourself.
scholar_explanation: Svātma is described as siddha, already accomplished, and as the sāra of svatantra-ānanda-vijñāna, echoing Kashmir Śaiva doctrines of the self-luminous, autonomous consciousness. Āveśana in tat-svarūpa functions like an internal snāna, a ritualized inner purification by recognition rather than water. The verse compresses the path into nondual identity with one's own essence.

speaker: Unknown
title: The Worshiper and Worship Become One
sanskrit:
यैरेव पूज्यते द्रव्यैस्तप्यन्ते वा परापरः ।
यश्चैव पूजकः सिद्धः स एवैकः क्व पूजनम् ॥ १५३ ॥
transliteration:
yai revā pūjyate dravyais tapyante vā parāparaḥ |
yaś caiva pūjakaḥ siddhaḥ sa evāikaḥ kva pūjanam || 153 ||
translation: By the very substances with which the Supreme and the relative are worshiped, or by which they are propitiated, that perfected worshiper is already the one alone—so where is there any worship?
intent_summary: To dissolve the distinction between worshiper, worshiped, and ritual means by revealing that realization itself is the only true fulfillment.
beginner_explanation: This verse points out that if everything is already one reality, then the person worshiping and the thing being worshiped are not truly separate. Once that is seen, the idea of 'I am offering this to God' loses its usual meaning. It is like discovering that the person in the mirror and the one looking are not two different beings.
scholar_explanation: The verse undermines the triad of pūjaka, pūjya, and upacāra by asserting the siddha worshiper as eka, the sole reality. This is a direct nondual critique of ritual dualism: the means of worship are not denied, but their ultimate separateness is sublated in realization. It resonates with later Śaiva views that external worship culminates in internal identity.

speaker: Unknown
title: Breath Moving by Will
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
व्रजेत् प्राणो विशेज्जीि इच्छया कुवटलाकृवत् ।
दीघाधत्मा सा महादेिी परक्षेिम् परापरा ॥ १५४ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairi tantram
vrajēt prāṇo viśej jīva icchayā kuṭilākṛt |
dīrghātmā sā mahādevī para-kṣetraṃ parāparā || 154 ||
translation: By will, the prāṇa goes forth and the living being enters, with a winding form. That long-bodied one is Mahādevī, the supreme and relative field.
intent_summary: To contemplate the subtle movement of prāṇa and jīva as expressions of the Goddess's own vast life-force.
beginner_explanation: This verse describes the breath and life-force moving in and out as if they were guided by a deeper intelligence. By observing that movement, you can sense that your own breathing is not just a mechanical function but part of a greater living presence. The image of a winding form suggests a subtle current moving through you.
scholar_explanation: Prāṇa and jīva are said to move by icchā, indicating the primacy of will as a śakti of consciousness. The 'kuṭilākṛti' evokes the coiling, subtle dynamism of power, while Mahādevī is identified as the para-kṣetra, the transcendent-immanent field in which such movements occur. This verse bridges breath practice with Śākta metaphysics.

speaker: Unknown
title: Hamsa Mantra and Breath Ingression
sanskrit:
अस्यामनुचरन् वतष्ठन् महानन्दमयेऽर्ध्वरे ।
तया देव्या समाविष्ट् परं भैरिं आप्नुयात् ॥ १५५ ॥
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सकारेण िवहयाधवत हकारेण विशेत् पुनः ।
हंसहंसेत्यमुं मन्त्रं जीिो जपति वनत्यश् ॥ १५५ ॥
transliteration:
asyāmanucarann tiṣṭhan mahānandamaye 'dhvare |
tayā devyā samāviṣṭaḥ paraṃ bhairavam āpnuyāt || 155 ||
sakāreṇa vahir yāvat hakāreṇa viśet punaḥ |
hamsaḥ hamsety amuṃ mantraṃ jīvo japati nityaśḥ || 155 ||
translation: Continuing in this way and remaining in the sacrifice filled with great bliss, one, entered by that Goddess, attains the supreme Bhairava. With sa one goes out, and with ha one enters again; the living being constantly recites this mantra, 'hamsa, hamsa.'
intent_summary: To use the natural in-breath and out-breath as a living mantra for entering the blissful presence of Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: This verse teaches a simple breath meditation: notice the out-breath as 'sa' and the in-breath as 'ha.' The breath itself becomes a mantra that is always happening, even when you are not trying. By staying with it, you can feel the breath become a doorway into deep peace and presence.
scholar_explanation: The hamsa-japa is framed as an automatic, continuous mantra generated by breathing: sa outward and ha inward. The practitioner remains in the mahānandamaya adhvara, a sacrificial space of bliss, and by that devī-samāveśa attains paraṃ bhairavam. This verse is central for breath-mantra integration in the VBT and later Haṃsa traditions.

speaker: Unknown
title: Countless Breath Mantra Practice
sanskrit:
षट्शतावन वदिा रािौ सहस्राण्येकविम्शवत् ।
जपो देव्याः समुवद्दष्टः सुलभो दुर्लभो जडैः ॥ १५६ ॥
transliteration:
ṣaṭśatāni divā rātrau sahasrāṇi ekaviṃśatiḥ |
japo devyāḥ samuddiṣṭaḥ sulabho durlabho jaḍaiḥ || 156 ||
translation: The goddess's recitation is declared to be six hundred by day and night, and twenty-one thousand by the thousands; it is easy for the awakened, but hard for the dull.
intent_summary: To indicate that the natural mantra of the breath is continuous and universally present, though only noticed by a sensitive practitioner.
beginner_explanation: This verse gives numbers to show how often the breath mantra happens all day and night. The point is not to count obsessively, but to realize that life is already repeating a sacred rhythm constantly. People who pay attention can notice it easily; others miss it.
scholar_explanation: The verse refers to the traditional count of breath cycles and the natural japa of the devī, here equated with the spontaneous hamsa recitation. The distinction between sulabha and durlabha-jaḍa underscores that realization depends on sensitivity and attentiveness, not merely on technique. This also links prāṇic rhythm with mantra-sādhana.

speaker: Unknown
title: Secrecy of the Supreme Nectar
sanskrit:
इत्येतद्विवततं देवि परमामृतमुत्तमम् ।
एतच्च नैव कस्यापि प्रकाश्यं तु कदाचन ॥ १५७ ॥
transliteration:
ity etad vistaritaṃ devi paramāmṛtam uttamam |
etac ca naiva kasyāpi prakāśyaṃ tu kadācana || 157 ||
translation: Thus this supreme and excellent nectar, O Goddess, has been expounded in detail. Yet this must never be revealed to just anyone at any time.
intent_summary: To warn that these teachings are precious and should be given only to suitable, receptive students.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the teaching is very valuable and not meant for casual sharing. Some things are meant to be given only when a person is ready to understand and use them properly. It is like giving medicine only to someone who knows how to take it safely.
scholar_explanation: The text characterizes the VBT teaching as paramāmṛta, a supreme nectar, but stresses esoteric transmission. The injunction against indiscriminate disclosure reflects tantric guru-disciple confidentiality and the concern that improper recipients may misunderstand or misuse the method. This is a standard closure marker in Tantric literature.

speaker: Unknown
title: Do Not Give to the Hostile or Cruel
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
परवशष्ये खले क्रूरे अभिे गुरुपादयो् ।
वनविधकल्पमतीनां तु िीराणां उन्नतात्मनाम् ॥ १५८ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
paraviśiṣye khale krūre abhakte gurupādayoḥ |
niviḍakalpamatīnāṃ tu vīrāṇāṃ unnatātmanām || 158 ||
translation: Not to an unworthy disciple, nor to the vile, cruel, or irreverent toward the guru's feet, but rather to heroic persons of lofty spirit whose minds are free from dense conceptualization.
intent_summary: To specify the kind of student fit for receiving the teaching: noble, brave, and not trapped in rigid thinking.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the teaching is not for people who are hostile, cruel, or disrespectful. It is for those who are strong inside, open-minded, and able to receive something subtle. A teaching like this needs a good container, like water needs a clean vessel.
scholar_explanation: The verse contrasts paraviśiṣya with khala and krūra, emphasizing ethical and contemplative suitability. Niviḍa-kalpamatīnāṃ negates those dominated by heavy conceptual fabrication, while vīrāṇāṃ unnatātmanām describes the qualified sādhaka as heroic and elevated. The emphasis is on receptivity beyond mere intellectualism.

speaker: Unknown
title: Give It Without Doubt to Devotees
sanskrit:
भिानां गुरुिगधस्य दातव्यं वनविधशङ्कया ।
ग्रामो राज्यं पुरं देश् पुिदारकुटुम्बकम् ॥ १५९ ॥
transliteration:
bhaktānāṃ guruvargasya dātavyaṃ niviḍaśaṅkayā |
grāmo rājyaṃ puraṃ deśaḥ putradāra-kuṭumbakam || 159 ||
translation: It should be given to devotees of the guru's lineage without doubt—having renounced village, kingdom, city, land, sons, wife, and family.
intent_summary: To instruct that the teaching belongs to those who are devoted and renounce worldly attachments.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the teaching should be given to sincere devotees who are ready to let go of strong attachments. It does not mean everyone must literally abandon their family, but that nothing should be more important than truth. The image is of someone willing to put aside social possessions and identities.
scholar_explanation: Bhaktānāṃ guruvargasya indicates transmission within a devotional and initiatory lineage, while the list of grāma through kuṭumbaka symbolizes renunciation of worldly identifications. The verse highlights that the teaching is safeguarded by both devotion and detachment, a common tantric criterion for secrecy and success. Its language also echoes renunciatory rhetoric without requiring external monasticism in every reading.

speaker: Unknown
title: Abandon All Else and Hold to This
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सिधमेतत्पवरत्यज्य ग्राह्यमेतन्मृगेक्षणे ।
वकमेवभरवस्थरैदेवि वस्थरं परवमदं धनम् ॥ १६० ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
sarvam etat parityajya grāhyam etan mṛgekṣaṇe |
kimeva bhairavasthairyair devi sthiraṃ param idaṃ dhanam || 160 ||
translation: Abandon all this and take hold of this, O deer-eyed one. What indeed is more stable than Bhairava-stability, O Goddess? This supreme treasure is steady.
intent_summary: To urge complete relinquishment of everything else in favor of the stable realization of Bhairava-consciousness.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to drop all other concerns and grasp the one thing that is truly steady. It says that the greatest treasure is not money or status, but an inner steadiness that does not change. Think of it as choosing the one support that never fails.
scholar_explanation: The imperative sarvam etat parityajya marks a decisive shift from worldly concerns to the stable ground of Bhairava-sthairya. The verse frames realization as sthiraṃ param dhanaṃ, the highest wealth, suggesting that the nondual state is not fleeting ecstasy but unwavering identity with the absolute. This serves as a concluding exhortation to prioritize the teaching over all conditional goods.

speaker: Unknown
title: Devi Declares Her Satisfaction
sanskrit:
प्राणा अवप प्रदातव्या न देयं परमामृतम् ।
श्री देव्युवाच ।
देिदेि माहदेि पवरतृप्तावस्म शङ्कर ॥ १६१ ॥
transliteration:
prāṇā avapa pradātavyā na deyaṃ paramāmṛtam |
śrī devy uvāca |
devi devi mahādevi paritṛptāsmi śaṅkara || 161 ||
translation: The life-forces may be given away, but the supreme nectar should not be given. The blessed Goddess said: 'Devi, Devi, Mahādevi, Śaṅkara, I am fully satisfied.'
intent_summary: This verse closes the teaching by stating that the highest truth is too precious to be casually given and acknowledging complete fulfillment in the teaching received.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that ordinary vitality or effort can be offered up, but the deepest nectar of realization is not something to hand out lightly. Devi then expresses that she is completely satisfied by what has been revealed. It feels like the end of a long lesson where the student says, 'I have received enough.'
scholar_explanation: The line distinguishes prāṇa from paramāmṛta, implying that the supreme nondual essence is not an object of transmission in the ordinary sense. Devi’s address to Śaṅkara and her declaration of paritṛptā indicate full assimilation of the instruction, a common Tantric closure in which revelation culminates in internal completion rather than further exposition. The verse belongs to the concluding dialogue rather than the dhāraṇās proper.

speaker: Unknown
title: Essence of the Vijñāna Bhairava
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरि तन्त्रम्
रुद्रयामलतन्त्रस्य सारमद्यािधावरतम् ।
सिधशविप्रभेदानां हृदयं ज्ञातमद्य च ॥ १६२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairavaṃ tantram |
rudrayāmalatantrasya sāram adyādhāritam |
siddhaśivaprabhेदānāṃ hṛdayaṃ jñātam adya ca || 162 ||
translation: This is the Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra. Today its essence of the Rudrayāmala Tantra has been upheld. Today, too, the heart of the distinctions among perfected Śivas has been known.
intent_summary: This verse identifies the text as the distilled essence of a larger Tantra and as the heart of realized Śiva-knowledge.
beginner_explanation: Here the text names itself and says it contains the essential teaching gathered from a larger tradition. It also says that the core of the wisdom of accomplished yogis or perfected Śivas has been understood. In other words, this is the verse that says, 'This is the heart of the matter.'
scholar_explanation: The verse explicitly self-identifies as the Vijñānabhairava Tantra and presents itself as sāra of the Rudrayāmala, a standard Tantric claim of textual condensation and legitimacy. The phrase siddhaśivaprabhेदānāṃ hṛdayam suggests the innermost essence or heart of the modes of perfected Śiva, emphasizing doctrinal centrality rather than mere literary closure. It reinforces the text’s role as a direct manual of nondual recognition and practice.

speaker: Unknown
title: Embrace and Final Blessing
sanskrit: इत्युक्त्वानवन्दता देवि कण्ठे लिा वशिस्य तु ॥ १६३ ॥
transliteration: ity uktvā nanandatā devī kaṇṭhe lagnā śivasya tu || 163 ||
translation: Having spoken thus, the Goddess rejoiced and clung to Śiva’s neck.
intent_summary: This final verse seals the teaching with intimacy, joy, and union between the Goddess and Śiva.
beginner_explanation: The story ends with Devi feeling joyful and embracing Śiva. This is a symbol of closeness and union, showing that the teaching has brought the two into complete harmony. It is like the final image in a story where everything comes together in love and understanding.
scholar_explanation: The closing image of devī lagnā kaṇṭhe śivasya evokes intimate nondual union, a symbolic resolution of the dialogue into embodied intimacy. Rather than ending with abstract doctrine, the text concludes with rasa-like fulfillment, indicating that knowledge (vijñāna) culminates in lived identity with Śiva. This functions as both narrative closure and an implicit blessing for transmission.
